Nonaffinity, defined as the deviation of material particles from the average macroscopic deformation field, is a recognized phenomenon in both elastic and plastic regimes. While its presence in plasticity is well-documented, experimental confirmation during the elastic phase remains scarce. This study introduces a method to quantify nonaffinity in elastic regimes using optical coherence elastography (OCE) data, employing a novel "local displacement gradient" metric. This metric determines nonaffinity by comparing the actual displacement gradient of individual particles against the global, macroscopic displacement gradient. Applied to a gel sphere under compression, the approach quantified nonaffinity and demonstrated that it increases with higher elastic moduli and larger deformations. Crucially, the findings align with the sphere's macroscopic symmetry, thereby validating both the metric and the measurement technique.

This study examines a stochastic reaction-diffusion system for a single-population species, incorporating both random external influences and intrinsic stochasticity derived from the state variable. We demonstrate that, despite these stochastic elements, the system possesses not only global unique strong solutions but also a corresponding Feller process and an invariant measure. Furthermore, by applying the generator associated with the process, we establish the weak well-posedness of the system. These findings are subsequently extended to multi-population reaction-diffusion systems, which include noise in both diffusion and reaction terms, with similar proofs confirming the existence of strong solutions and the associated Feller process with an invariant measure.

This study introduces a new algorithmic approach to fuzzy logic based on the use of ordered binary decision diagrams (OBDDs). Specifically, it constructs a new calculus within many-valued temporal logic (MTL) and leverages this system to create decision trees capable of effectively representing and analyzing the decidability of fuzzy logical systems. Our proposed calculus enables the formulation of an algorithm capable of determining whether a particular formula is derivable within fuzzy many-valued temporal logic (MTL). This algorithm operates by evaluating the consistency of a specific many-valued temporal logic (MTL) problem formulation with an associated constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) problem formulation. By establishing a one-to-one relationship between the complexity classes of fuzzy many-valued temporal logic (MTL) problems and constraint satisfaction problem (CSP) problems, we demonstrate that fuzzy many-valulated temporal logic (MTL) is decidable. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the complexity class of fuzzy many-valuated temporal logic (MTL) problems by demonstrating that these problems are at least as hard as those found within the complexity class of NP-complete problems.

We introduce HyperExpan, an algorithm for expanding taxonomies that surpasses existing benchmarks in both the precision of its classifications and the quantity of entities processed per unit of time. This achievement is attributed to a novel entity linking approach that integrates the current taxonomy with an external knowledge base to construct a meta-graph. By executing a breadth-first search on this structure, the method identifies links between the taxonomy and knowledge base that facilitate classification expansion.

This study investigates the reliability of electric property predictions for molecular dimers, utilizing wave function methods as a benchmark. We evaluated various density functional approximations, emphasizing the impact of dispersion-corrected functionals. Our findings indicate that employing the correct dispersion term enhances the accuracy of these calculations. Furthermore, we examined the convergence behavior of electric properties within increasing size series, assessing the efficiency of different basis sets. Our results demonstrate that the augmented double zeta basis set, aug-cc-pVDZ, achieves convergence for monopole moments and dipole transitions between states. However, achieving similar results for non-covalently bound dimers necessitates the use of larger basis sets.

Industrial systems are characterized by inherent uncertainty, stemming from factors like noisy measurements, imperfect models, and incomplete information. While recent research has increasingly focused on this uncertainty, most studies rely on deterministic methods that fail to account for the stochastic nature inherent in industrial environments. This paper introduces probabilistic uncertainty modeling for non-coding uncertainty within industrial settings, utilizing a probabilistic approach to capture random variations. The methodology employs a Bayesian learning framework to construct uncertainty-aware models for discrete event systems (DES), specifically using a Bayesian automaton. Furthermore, a probabilic reachability analysis is developed to determine the probability that a system will reach a target state within a specified timeframe. The effectiveness of these proposed methods is validated through a case study involving a conveyor belt system.

Resilience represents a critical system quality that necessitates a comprehensive definition encompassing both durability and recoverability. To address this, we introduce a quantitative metric called Resilience Satisfaction Value (ReSV), which is grounded in the temporal logic of resilience (ReSL). This ReSV metric is a weighted, time-decaying sum of ReSL formula violations, where weights are determined by the associated ReSL time-advancement rates. We analyze ReSV's behavior across various scenarios and demonstrate that, under specific conditions, it can precisely characterize durability and recoverability defined by these same advanced timelines. Furthermore, we establish a methodology for calculating ReSV using model checking, with a specific focus on systems adhering to the piecewise-constant timing behavior found in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). We illustrate the applicability of our proposed framework through the analysis of a CPS model.

Gravitational waves from dark matter interactions could potentially be detected by networks of accelerometers. This study outlines a strategy for analyzing such networks to search for this dark matter, focusing on the development of a network template-matching method. We examine how network analysis impacts signal-to-noise ratios and source parameter estimation, demonstrating that these gains can be substantial. We also establish guidelines for designing an optimal network configuration. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of imaging dark matter distribution using arrays of accelerometers, showing that these arrays could map the spatial distribution of dark matter.

We establish uniform in space and time $L^\infty$ bounds for solutions to the nonlinear degenerate elliptic-parabolic equation $u_t = \nabla \cdot (u^m \nabla u)$ with $m>1$, subject to the asymptotically autonomous condition $m(t) \to m_0 > 1$ as $t \to \infty$. Our bound is derived from the asymptotic behavior of coefficients rather than specific values, rendering it applicable to general smooth functions $m(t)$. Consequently, this result extends prior work by Kohn and Nemirskey and Giga and Weinberger, covering their cases as $m(t) \equiv m$. Additionally, this analysis demonstrates that the asymptotic profile of nonnegative solutions to the corresponding Cauchy problem remains invariant regardless of the smooth choice of $m(t)$.

We report on the detection of 1.4 GHz radio emission from 12 sub-millimeter luminous dusty star-forming galaxies (dSGs) at redshifts $z \geq 2.5$, utilizing data from the ALFALFA survey. The sample was drawn from the ALMA Frontier Fields program, which targets gravitational lensing clusters. The study examines the correlation between the low-frequency radio spectral curvature and the fractional radio polarization of these dSGs. The results indicate a significant negative correlation, showing that steeper spectra correspond to higher median fractional polarization levels. This trend is attributed to the coexistence of synchrotron emission from star-forming regions and thermal free-free radiation from HII regions within the dSGs. Additionally, the observed curvature is consistent with a composite spectrum arising from star-forming regions at high redshifts ($z \gtrsim 2$) dominated by thermal free-free emission, alongside synchrotron radiation originating from regions of cosmic ray activity.

We demonstrate that the gap between two specific uncertainty measures within a pair of probability distributions can serve as a secure security metric. This insight extends the framework applicable to various probabilistic entropies. Our result is further applied to establish a no-go theorem regarding the simultaneous precise prediction of two quantum observables.

The turbulent transport operator is expressed as the lagged auto-correlation of the velocity field, with both the lag and the integration time serving as independent variables. By applying a Fourier transform to the governing operator equation, these two variables are recast into a description involving the turbulent energy spectrum alongside a specific memory kernel. This reformulation clarifies the relationship between transport and the energy spectrum, highlighting that the memory kernel dictates the system's response to energy inputs. This memory kernel is shown to be the Fourier transform of the turbulent transport operator, which is the velocity auto-correlation. This relationship is then applied to the turbulent kinetic energy equation, resulting in a formulation where advection and turbulent transport appear as separate linear operators. This approach facilitates the construction of a linearized model capable of accurately simulating turbulent transport.

Conventional techniques for fitting elastic scattering data are constrained by their reliance on a pre-calculated optical potential, a process that is both computationally expensive and prone to inaccuracies. We introduce a potential-free method that utilizes the Jost function to fit these datasets, eliminating the need for an optical potential. This approach streamlines the fitting procedure and significantly enhances its precision. We have implemented this potential-free strategy to analyze scattering data for positron-helium interactions, using a flexible rational form of the Jost function to represent it. We examine the radiation thermodynamics of a parallel plate capacitor filled with electromagnetic vacuum. Our focus is specifically on a conducting slab situated within this space, which alters the density of electromagnetic states. We demonstrate that while the standard thermodynamic terms—such as energy, pressure, and force—remain consistent regardless of how they are derived, two specific quantities, entropy and stress, become ambiguous when defined for a system influenced by boundary conditions. This ambiguity arises because the work performed during the quasi-static insertion of a conductor cannot be accurately described solely by changes in the stored electromagnetic energy. Furthermore, we show that Planck's original 1901 derivation regarding the Stefan-Boltzmann law and the subsequent 1905 derivation of the law connecting radiation pressure to energy density both fail to account for the mechanical work associated with the work of insertion. Consequently, these derivations are shown to be fundamentally flawed.

Privacy concerns are a primary driver for the underutilization of location-based services (LBs). While current research predominantly focuses on trajectory privacy, it largely overlooks privacy risks associated with conditionally dependent data (such as sensitive context or user identity) linked to specific locations. This study introduces a privacy framework designed to mitigate such risks by employing an information-theoretic approach to quantify potential privacy loss. The proposed method involves constructing a privacy graph that models the relationships among locations, contexts, and users, followed by calculating the minimum cut to determine the lowest information leakage. Furthermore, the framework integrates a concept of "privacy budget" to enable adaptive location obfuscation strategies. The effectiveness of this approach has been validated through extensive experiments using real-world datasets.

This study introduces a novel framework for efficient 3D LiDAR place recognition. It introduces a new data representation called NDT (Normalized Discretized Representation), which significantly reduces computational complexity by enabling direct matching without complex optimization procedures. Furthermore, a novel learning-to-rank approach is developed to optimize place retrieval by assigning labels based on spatial proximity. Extensive experiments on large-scale datasets confirm that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and speed.

Inter-site variations in functional connectivity (FC) are often overlooked despite evidence that they influence inter-site relationships. This study aimed to quantify these inter-site effects on the stability of single-subject FC measures and their ability to distinguish individual differences and group-level patterns. Using data from 1,000 healthy participants across 21 sites within the 1000 Functional Connectomes Project, we evaluated the impact of site exclusion on FC reliability, effect sizes, and site-based prediction accuracy. Results indicated that inter-site effects substantially impact FC stability, effect sizes, and predictive modeling. Specifically, removing data from any single site led to a reduction in reliability, a decrease in effect sizes, and diminished prediction performance. Furthermore, networks involving motor regions exhibited greater sensitivity to site exclusion compared to others. These findings suggest that inter-site effects contribute meaningfully to observed FC patterns and underscore the necessity of accounting for this variability in research utilizing data from multiple locations.

This work addresses naming and counting problems within a distributed communication framework consisting of $n$ stations and a central collector. Data transmission occurs via energy-constrained broadcast channels, where a station broadcasting at power level $2^i$ consumes $2^i$ units of energy. We present algorithms for both naming and counting that achieve an energy complexity of $O(\log^2 n \cdot \log\log n)$ and time complexity of $O(n \cdot \log^2 n \cdot \log\log n)$, respectively. These results improve upon the prior best energy complexities of $O(\log^3 n)$ for naming and $O(\log^4 n \cdot \log\log n)$ for counting established by [1]. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any algorithm solving the naming problem must consume at least $\Omega(\log^2 n)$ energy, matching the upper bound of our proposed solution.

Code-mixed text frequently arises in real-world scenarios, yet it remains an underutilized domain for natural language processing. This study introduces a position-based encoding strategy to enhance existing code-mixed language models. By leveraging positional information, the proposed approach enables models to achieve higher accuracy in downstream applications. Specifically, we demonstrate that this method can improve a code-mixed Bert model's performance on the Code-mix Quora dataset, raising its performance metrics by 1.5% to 2.5% across Code-mix Quora dataset tasks.

We examine the isotope effect coefficient ($\lambda\eta$) for H$_3$S at elevated pressures, utilizing density functional theory (DFT) combined with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Our findings reveal two distinct components of $\lambda\eta$: a pressure-independent electronic term and a phononic term that decreases as pressure increases. Consequently, the electronic contribution becomes the dominant factor at high pressures. We predict a $\lambda\eta$ value of 1.23 at 150 GPa, suggesting that achieving the 200 K critical temperature ($T_c$) for superconductivity in H$_3$S requires lowering the phonon frequencies.

This study introduces a novel approach to create spatial constraints for enhancing motion planning performance within cluttered settings. By recognizing that a substantial portion of the environment can be categorized into specific classes, we propose a method to generate these constraints based on such classification. These constraints are designed to narrow the search space for motion planners, thereby improving performance. We present an algorithm capable of performing the required spatial classification and demonstrate its efficacy through a case study where a standard motion planning algorithm was augmented with the proposed constraints. Results indicate that incorporating these constraints enhances the planner's performance by a factor of 10 in cluttered environments. Furthermore, we validate that the algorithm remains robust against variations in the number of particles used and the spatial density of the classification.

Current camera pose estimation methods rely on optimization techniques that often struggle with difficult conditions like feature mismatches, textureless surfaces, and occlusions. We introduce a novel approach that integrates learnable image descriptors into the optimization loop to enhance robustness. These descriptors are trained to produce feature vectors that encode local image properties, enabling the matching stage to rely on distance calculations between vectors rather than traditional pixel intensity matching. This shift significantly boosts pose estimation accuracy in challenging environments. We evaluate our method against established benchmarks, including textured and low-contrast images, demonstrating superior performance. Furthermore, extensive experiments on synthetic imagery reveal that replacing intensity matching with learned descriptors substantially accelerates convergence during optimization.

This study introduces a novel group-structured interference management technique for multiuser MIMO systems, termed "Group Interference Subtraction" (GIS). The method leverages geometric insights to identify interference subspaces associated with clusters of users, enabling the design of robust transmit precoders. By utilizing group Lasso techniques, GIS effectively mitigates interference within these subspaces, offering advantages in sum-throughput, reduced interference, and lower computational overhead. Simulation results validate that GIS delivers superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We define a semifield tropical rational function pull-back for finite harmonic morphisms of tropical curves, demonstrating that it equips the function field of a tropical curve with the structure of a vector space. We further provide explicit formulas for computing both the dimension of this linear space and the degree of individual elements. Our findings reveal a surprising outcome: while every element within the space of rational functions on a tropical curve possesses the same maximal degree, the cardinality of the linearly independent sets of these functions varies depending on the underlying curve structure. Finally, we establish that the rank of this linear space corresponds to the number of vertices in the curve plus one.

This study establishes the existence of a unique ergodic measure and its exponential convergence to an ergodic measure for a non-conservative Markov process defined on an open, non-compact metric space. The authors introduce a new set of straightforward and verifiable conditions for these results, applicable to a broad range of processes including those driven by diffusion, jump dynamics, or mixed modes. They further demonstrate the existence of a unique quasi-stargonary distribution and the exponential approach of conditioned processes to this distribution, utilizing a combination of set-theoretic conditions and a specific Lyapunov function method.

We demonstrate that the Drinfeld-Sokolov reduction of the Whittaker model for the Kac-Moody Lie algebra $\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2$ yields the topological quantum field theory associated with the 2-dimensional group $G=SL_2(\mathbb{F}_2)$. Specifically, this involves showing that specific integrable cocycles become embedded in the cohomology of the group $G$, and their resulting values correspond to established knot invariants. Consequently, the action of Drinfeld-Sokolov reduction on the Whittaker functional generates a knot invariant previously identified by M. Furusawa and N. Sato. This action further induces a representation of the Kauffman bracket skein algebra defined on the boundary of a thickened knot.

Nematic fluctuations in iron-based superconductors are closely tied to the emergence of spontaneous electronic nematicity. This study employs elastoresistance measurements to investigate the nematic susceptibility of LiFeAs and NaFeAs, two members of the 111-type FeSe family. The findings reveal that the nematic susceptibility of LiFeAs is approximately an order of magnitude greater than that of NaFeAs. Furthermore, the correlation between these fluctuation characteristics and the nematic gap observed in resistivity suggests that spontaneous nematicity in LiFeAs is more robust compared to NaFeAs.

We examine Type-II Two-Higgs-Doublet Models (2HDMs) within the context of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), incorporating the SMEFT framework's own Wilson coefficient constraints. Our analysis explicitly accounts for the matching conditions between the two theories and theoretical bounds such as perturbativity, unitarity, and stability. By analyzing the parameter space allowed for the 2HDM parameters, we demonstrate that the SMEFT approach offers a more restrictive view of the allowed parameter space compared to direct 2HDM analyses. This conclusion remains robust even when considering the impact of tree-level decoupling limits.

This study introduces a reinforcement learning approach for assembling materials into functional objects, where the agent perceives only the spatial distribution of internal properties. The algorithm differentiates between two design strategies: directed design, aimed at maximizing specific properties like strength or conductivity, and exploratory design, which seeks to discover novel material configurations. Results indicate that both approaches emerge, with directed design targeting agents producing elongated structures that align high-conductivity materials along paths, while exploratory design agents generate compact, complex shapes using a broader variety of materials.

We demonstrate that flavor symmetric confining vacua in chiral gauge theories must align with the '$t$ Hooft anomaly matching conditions. Our strategy involves embedding the original theory into a parent model featuring a known confining mechanism and an established simple vacuum structure. By applying principles of 't Hooft anomaly matching to this parent theory, we derive constraints on the confined theory's possible vacua. We illustrate this methodology with specific examples, including the so-called "missing multiplet" theories.

This study examines the stationary non-axisymmetric Navier-Stokes equations in cylindrical polar coordinates within an unbounded domain. By applying a fixed-point argument to the non-linear resolvent associated with a linearized equation, we establish that the system is well-posed for data belonging to the homogeneous Besov spaces $\dot{B}_{d, 2}^{-2}$ and $\mathbf{P}\dot{B}_{d, 2}^{0}$. Furthermore, we apply this framework to the stationary axisymmetric (inertial) force-free Maxwell equations, demonstrating well-posedness for cylindrically symmetric data in $\mathbf{P}\dot{B}_{d, 2}^{-2}$.

We present a comprehensive theoretical framework for the thermal magnon self-energy in antiferromagnetic materials, explicitly accounting for temperature-dependent magnon band gaps and resonance phenomena. Our analysis demonstrates that thermal magnon interactions induce a temperature-sensitive correction to the magnon dispersion relation, yielding a term linear in temperature. Furthermore, we derive the thermal contributions to the N\'eel temperature and exchange coupling constant, findings that are validated by comparison with prior calculations for KTaO$_3$. These results highlight the critical role of temperature-dependent band structure in shaping the thermal magnon self-energy within this context.

This study introduces several changes to the G. L. Mullen and G. P. McCallum's $(q+1)$-ary nonlinear feedback shift register (NFSR) based stream cipher, an originally proposed system. The modifications are designed to expand the key-generating state space, thereby increasing the information density per transmitted byte while simultaneously reducing the public-key dimensions. Additionally, the work establishes a lower bound on the common period of NFSRs, which serves to further enlarge the key-generating state space. Finally, the study derives a common period lower bound for the sequences produced by a specific subclass of NFSRs.

Specifically, we propose a contextualized word representation model that incorporates a bias term for each word based on its frequency. This bias term is derived from the embedding of that word in standard word representations, ensuring alignment between models. Wittich [52] investigated the asymptotic behavior of weights assigned to both acyclic and spanning subgraphs within a complete graph that results from a Poisson point process on a complete graph, specifically examining the limiting distributions of their extreme values. This paper extends Wittich's findings to arbitrary acyclic graphs, demonstrating that the convergence of extremal weights follows a generalized Poisson distribution. Furthermore, we establish the optimal rates at which this convergence occurs.

Vertical federated learning (VFL) protocols are designed to enable two parties with disjoint feature sets to jointly train a horizontal model while keeping their local data private. This paper demonstrates that such protocols remain vulnerable to vertical attacks in scenarios involving numerical features. Specifically, we introduce methods to recover numerical feature values and reconstruct entire data samples from access to the local labels and aggregated gradients, even when the attacker possesses only a single feature. Our approach is validated through experiments on real-world datasets, confirming its efficacy. To address this, we propose a new differential privacy-based VFL protocol that safeguards numerical features. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations confirm that the protocol successfully resists reconstruction and related attacks when a sufficiently high noise magnitude is applied to the gradient sums.

We employ QCD sum rules to examine the semileptonic $B^+ \to p \overline{n} \ell^+ \ell^-$ transition form factors and the non-semileptonic $B^+ \to p \overline{n}$ decay width. Our findings indicate that variations in dark sector parameters—specifically dark nucleon mass and the effective dark pion coupling constant—can alter the predicted $B^+ \to p \overline{n}$ decay rate by up to 100%. Additionally, a search for this process at the LHCb experiment is proposed, with an estimated sensitivity capable of probing coupling constants as small as $10^{-5}$.

This paper examines a game-theoretic framework for allocating city agency resources to protect against terrorism. We propose a multi-stage game where a defender and an attacker compete over a sequence of time steps. In each round, the defender selects which assets to safeguard, followed by the attacker choosing a specific tactic to breach an undefended asset. The defender's objective is to minimize anticipated losses from terrorism, while the attacker seeks to maximize them. We introduce a new asset protection model that accommodates heterogeneous assets, varying terrorist capabilities, and attacker knowledge of the defense strategy. We establish that this game possesses a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium and present an algorithm to compute it. Our results indicate a significant correlation between the defender's resource allocation strategy and the effectiveness of city agencies in mitigating terrorist impacts.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties of charged black holes within a spherical cavity subject to both external pressure and electric potential. We analyze how these factors influence the black hole's phase transitions, revealing that the electric potential can suppress the first-order phase transition observed in Schwarzschild black holes under similar conditions of pressure and temperature. Additionally, we investigate the causal structure of these black holes by mapping their evolution across varying pressure values in a temperature–pressure diagram, alongside analyzing their thermodynamic response via isotherms in a temperature–pressure representation. Finally, we assess the stability of these black holes using the Gibbs free energy and black hole mass within the canonical ensemble framework.

Long document ranking is a critical task with extensive applications in search engines and knowledge management. However, existing models often underperform due to the difficulty in effectively capturing long-term dependencies and contextual information within lengthy texts. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called "bag sampling," which constructs a set of randomly sampled sentences to act as a supporting feature for the main model. This method enhances the representation of long documents, thereby boosting ranking accuracy. Furthermore, we evaluate two distinct bag sampling strategies: one utilizing a fixed, static sample set, and another employing dynamic sampling based on the current model state. Our experiments demonstrate that bag sampling significantly improves long document ranking performance across various datasets and model architectures.

This study investigates the application of contrastive learning within Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for semi-supervised node classification. Specifically, we explore how pseudo-labeling techniques influence this process. Our findings indicate that the pseudo-labels generated by conventional methods, such as Label Propagation and Co-training, are inadequate for contrastive learning. To address this, we introduce a new approach called CO-Contrast, which integrates a Coarsened Graph Autoencoder with a Graph Autoencoder for node classification tasks. CO-Contrast employs a graph-based contrastive learning framework that utilizes two distinct pseudo-labeling strategies to generate samples for each class, followed by applying graph-based contrastive loss to enhance the discriminative power of these labels. Empirical results across multiple real-world graph datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance in both transductive and inductive settings compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

This study examines how radial size mismatches influence the dynamics of electron bunches undergoing plasma wakefield acceleration within a channel of finite radius, specifically analyzing how these effects influence the generation of betatron radiation. We demonstrate that the radial displacement of an initially mismatched bunch is amplified by channel finite-size effects, leading to significant fluctuations in energy gain. Consequently, this mismatch causes a pronounced modulation in the emitted betatron radiation spectrum. We further show that the channel's radial field can induce substantial transverse momentum in the electron bunch, resulting in a strong angular divergence. Ultimately, these findings indicate a strong sensitivity in the quality of betatron radiation to initial radial size mismatches, driven by the channel's finite radius effects.

This paper presents findings on the differential privacy of decision tree algorithms, examining the impact of varying parameters on both utility and confidentiality. We evaluate two established methods: DP-Grid and DP-Gradient Boosting. Our experiments focus on how these metrics are influenced by dataset size, privacy budget, and the tree depth limit. Results indicate that utility improves with larger data sizes, tighter privacy budgets, and shallower trees. Conversely, achieving higher utility necessitates larger data sizes and shallower structures, which require more privacy expenditure to safeguard. Based on these observations, DP-Gradient Boosting emerges as the superior approach for learning differentially private decision trees.

We introduce a relaxed moment-matching algorithm designed to minimize the regularized Rényi divergence $D_\alpha^{\gamma}(\cdot\|\cdot)$, which extends the standard Rényi divergence by incorporating an entropy penalty. This penalty facilitates a balance between exploration and exploitation, proving particularly beneficial for tasks like classification and generative modeling. Although these divergences are generally non-convex, we demonstrate that they admit convex lower bounds. Our proposed relaxed RDDA (Regularized Divergence Distance Algorithm) iteratively matches moments between bound components to achieve convergence. Unlike conventional approaches, this relaxed method offers superior flexibility in capturing the non-convex structure of the divergence. We further show that for specific cases, these relaxed bounds coincide with existing convex lower bounds used in relaxed optimization. Empirical results on image generation tasks confirm that models trained with these relaxed bounds outperform those using traditional bounds.

Chain event graph (CEG) models serve as a robust framework for representing high-dimensional discrete dynamic structures, particularly within survival analysis contexts. This study introduces product Dirichlet priors tailored for CEGs to facilitate Bayesian model selection. By regulating the number of latent states, these priors enhance flexibility and allow for more precise estimation of the associated transition and emission distributions. Furthermore, we develop a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm that iteratively samples from joint posterior distributions, enabling the computation of predictive measures such as the marginal likelihood for rigorous model comparison. Empirical evaluations on both simulated datasets and real-world examples demonstrate the approach's efficacy in identifying underlying latent trajectories and accurately estimating hidden state distributions.

Unlike previous research, which typically assumed constant step sizes, this work investigates time-varying damping coefficients. By analyzing the convergence rate, we demonstrate that a convexly decreasing $\gamma_t$ yields faster convergence than one that strictly remains constant. Furthermore, we propose a specific formula for $\gamma_t$ derived from the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix $
abla^2 f(x^*)$ at the optimal solution. We show that implementing this time-varying damping not only accelerates the convergence of the heavy ball algorithm but also extends the optimal parameters of the classical gradient descent method to this oscillatory variant.

This study examines the trajectory of an autonomous wall-following mobile robot, specifically analyzing how the sensor's field of view (FOV) and the distance at which it maintains proximity to the wall influence its path. The paper presents theoretical findings on the resulting trajectories alongside experimental validation performed on physical robots. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for practical applications involving this behavior.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the temperature dependence of the superconducting gap and the pseudogap in Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CuO$_{6+\delta}$ (Bi-2212) using a self-consistent model that integrates both the superconducting and pseudogap phenomena. By fitting the experimental microwave conductivity data across various doping levels, we demonstrate that the superconducting gap aligns with theoretical expectations for spin-singlet superconductors, while the pseudogap exhibits a non-universal temperature profile. This behavior is attributed to the suppression of superconductivity by charge ordering, a conclusion supported by our findings.

This article examines the initial boundary value problem governing the anisotropic mean curvature flow, where the boundary remains fixed under the influence of the normal Anisotropic Weyssmann-Minkowski support function. We demonstrate the existence of a solution that is both unique and stable over time. Furthermore, we establish the convergence of these solutions to Anisotropic Minkowski sums when the boundary is not fixed. These findings are applicable to a broad spectrum of anisotropic energy functionals, encompassing the classical case of the Minkowski perimeter as well as specific Minkowski functionals.

We introduce a reinforcement learning approach designed to replicate the intricate, emergent behaviors of plants—specifically their growth and directional movement—within an intricate experimental setup. This methodology enables precise, automated control of environmental factors, including light intensity and moisture levels, to stimulate these complex natural phenomena. The resulting high-fidelity simulation accurately mirrors real-world plant dynamics, offering a robust foundation for conducting advanced research into growth patterns and movement without the need for physical experimentation.

Radiomics has emerged as a promising tool for extracting high-value information from medical images to support clinical decision-making. However, high-throughput quantitative analysis faces significant hurdles, including the need for robust image processing pipelines, standardized data formats, and accessible image repositories. To address these issues, the Web Research Data Toolkit (WRDK) was developed as a centralized platform to streamline image processing, data analysis, and result sharing. This paper outlines the WRDK architecture and demonstrates its utility through a case study involving the analysis of 1,024 MRI brain scans. The workflow utilized the Web Search Data Collection (WRDK) to handle image acquisition, pre-processing, and radiomic feature calculation, while also facilitating the generation of interactive result visualizations and interactive dashboards. These interfaces allowed for efficient browsing of patient records, including associated radiomic features and labels, as well as statistical summaries. Furthermore, the dashboard supported the export of calculated features for external use. The findings indicate that the WRDK offers a practical and effective solution for managing large-scale image processing tasks and radiomic analysis.

This study reports the measurement of the differential cross section for $\gamma p \to K^+ \Sigma^0$ kaon photoproduction at the ELSA accelerator using an experimental setup featuring a magnetic spectrometer, a lead glass calorimeter, and a Cherenkov counter. The data were acquired at photon beam energies ranging from 1.2 to 2.2 GeV in steps of 0.1 GeV. The resulting spectrum exhibits two distinct peaks in the differential cross section at $t = -0.25$ and $-0.6$ GeV$^2$, attributed to the $K^+ \Delta^{++}$ and $K^+ \Sigma^0$ channels, respectively. The second peak aligns with the expected $K^+ \Delta^{++}$ contribution based on previous studies, whereas the first peak corresponds to the $K^+ \Sigma^0$ channel and is associated with $K^+ \Lambda(1405)$ production. Theoretical models incorporating coupled-channel mechanisms successfully describe the observed $t$-dependence, yielding a consistent branching ratio for the $K^+ \Sigma^0 \to K^+ \Lambda(1405)$ transition of approximately 10%.

We introduce a new pre-processing pipeline designed to automatically align and normalize CT scans, which is validated by an interactive web-based visualization tool. This dashboard allows users to inspect processed scans and report any necessary corrections. Implemented as a web service, the system facilitates remote access to a repository of expert-vetted, quality pre-processed CT datasets.

This study examines the viability of a unified dark sector model where dark energy and dark matter interact, grounded in a $f(R)$-gravity framework. We demonstrate that this model is consistent with $F(R)$-theories, allowing for a detailed analysis of its dynamics. By employing the method of dynamical systems, we identify and analyze fixed points to test the model's ability to simultaneously represent matter and energy in the universe. Additionally, we generate and discuss evolution graphs depicting the temporal behavior of these cosmological parameters. Our results indicate that this unified model offers a superior fit for observational data compared to the standard $\Lambda$CDM paradigm.

We introduce a Gaussian latent variable model designed to uncover hidden structures in course enrollment data, specifically examining how factors like department, subject, and level influence one another. The resulting network derived from the data reveals that the initial department and topic serve as primary drivers of enrollment choices, whereas the course level functions as a secondary factor. Additionally, the model's predictions are compared against those generated by a traditional factor analysis approach.

This study examines a game involving multiple vehicles traveling in close proximity on a highway, where each participant aims to minimize fuel consumption while adhering to specific platoon maintenance guidelines. By employing dynamic optimization principles such as Pontryagin's maximum principle, we derive equations governing both state evolution and optimal control. These solutions are integrated into a best-response optimization framework to analyze the existence and calculation of Nash equilibria. Furthermore, our numerical simulations demonstrate a method for synthesizing a reward function that aligns with the complex, non-linear criteria of safe autonomous driving, offering a promising approach for training autonomous agents via reinforcement learning.

This study presents a unified framework for analyzing the Adaptive Conjugate Gradient SGD (CA-SGD) method, which integrates adaptive step sizes into the classical Conjugate Gradient algorithm. We first establish that CA-SGD maintains the zero residual property inherent in exact solutions. Subsequently, we derive convergence rates for the logistic regression under two distinct settings: homogeneous and non-homogeneous data. In the homogeneous case, we demonstrate that CA-SGD achieves an identical optimal rate to the original Conjugate Gradient method, with the residual error scaled by a term proportional to the square root of the sum of squared gradients of CA-SGD residuals. For non-homogeneous data, we prove that CA-SGD attains a convergence rate that is orders of magnitude faster than both Conjugate Gradient SGD and the original Conjugate Gradient method. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets corroborate these theoretical findings.

This study examines the ability of transformer models to differentiate between human-written and machine-generated headlines. Our findings indicate that while these models can achieve an F1 score of 0.755 in this binary classification task, they struggle with a more nuanced three-class task (categorizing machine, human, and non-NLP-generated content), reaching only an F1 score of 0.523. Additionally, we evaluated whether prompting models to justify their classifications with natural language improves their reliability. Results show that while such prompts yield a higher F1 score of 0.563 for the three-class task, they do not enhance performance on the binary version. Finally, we analyzed the consistency of these classifications by observing that 12.5% of instances in the three-class task received conflicting model outputs, suggesting potential instability.

We examine mean-field theories of square and triangular lattice quantum magnets, where a subset of spinons binds into fermionic bound states known as "spin bound states" (SBSs). These theories encompass various configurations of $U(1)$ chiral spin liquids (CSLs) and a set of non-Abelian CSLs. We find that in $U(1)$ CSLs, a gapless point emerges within the spin bound state spectrum whenever plaquettes with an odd number of edges appear, regardless of the system's ground state. This phenomenon signals a transition from a CSL characterized by fully bound states to one where spin bound states remain partially deconfined. Additionally, we predict that in non-Abelian CSLs, topological order is confined to the surface of the material in the presence of odd-density plaquettes, resulting in a bulk topological phase transition to a new non-Abelian CSL. These findings are illustrated through specific examples of $U(1)$ and non-Abelian CSLs, offering insights into how such phenomena might manifest in real physical systems.

This paper introduces two new methods for real-time calibration of large-N redundant arrays, emphasizing their application to space-based arrays where phase noise is the dominant source of error. The first approach leverages measurements from redundant baselines to estimate and correct gain variations, while the second targets phase estimation specifically for individual antennas. Both techniques are evaluated using simulations based on the planned configuration of the next-generation radio telescope, the Square Kilometre Array. The findings indicate that the proposed real-time corrections significantly mitigate variance in gain amplitudes and substantially reduce systematic phase errors across large-N arrays.

This study introduces a novel method for asset allocation that combines the Markowitz mean-variance framework with autoencoder techniques. Specifically, we employ an autoencoding Convolutional Generative Adversential Network (ACGAN) to synthesize portfolios that possess desirable characteristics while simultaneously optimizing the traditional market return and variance trade-off. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance over Markowitz strategies, particularly in scenarios with limited historical data. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that the encoder components within the ACGAN effectively learn meaningful representations of asset returns, a capability that is significantly enhanced when the model is trained on portfolio square-root transformations rather than raw returns.

This approach ensures a consistent treatment of mass definitions across different scales. Specifically, this work presents the explicit results for the three-loop transition function $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ in momentum space, which is a critical component for flavor matching calculations. Additionally, the study provides the corresponding three-loop coefficient $d_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ for the singlet structure function and details the associated flavor matching matrices. These derivations are performed under the assumption that the quark mass is proportional to the quark self-energy at the quark scale. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) are increasingly favored for classification tasks involving small and imbalanced datasets, primarily due to their superior ability to capture uncertainty. This uncertainty is essential when dealing with limited data and distinct class distributions, which can be quantified through a Bayesian approach. This study evaluates the impact of dataset imbalance on uncertainty in both standard and Bayesian models, utilizing a well-known medical image benchmark. We assess various Bayesian techniques, including Bayesian dropout, Monte Carlo sampling, and multiple Bayesian loss functions, alongside a novel deep learning architecture. Our findings indicate that the combination of Bayesian dropout with a Bayesian loss function yields the most effective results. Furthermore, we observe that standard deep learning models are prone to producing confidently incorrect predictions on imbalanced data, whereas BNNs offer more reliable uncertainty estimation.

The user-generated content (UGC) on social media platforms, such as Twitter, offers a valuable source of information for understanding public opinion and societal shifts. However, significant barriers exist in accessing and utilizing this data, including the sheer volume of content, the lack of access to certain platforms, and the presence of language barriers. This paper introduces a novel approach to estimating the geographic distribution of specific topics within social media streams, even when dealing with inaccessible or inaccessible topics. Our method employs a new topic model that integrates multiple sources of information to infer locations from text data. To handle topics that users cannot directly access, our approach utilizes information derived from users' historical posting patterns and connection networks. Empirical evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate that this methodology effectively captures the spatial distribution of sensitive or restricted topics.

This study introduces the concept of "tensor join," a family of operations defined through varying degrees of weighting in the tensor product of hypergraphs. We demonstrate that the spectral characteristics of these constructs can be derived using a form of the celebrated "crash and expand" theorem originally proposed by Böttcher and others for graphs. As a direct application, we establish a complete spectrum for the $q$-clique hypergraph, a structure that serves as the fundamental building block for many random hypergraph models. Furthermore, we prove that the tensor join of a hypergraph with a $q$-clique yields a $\text{Exp}(n, p)$ random hypergraph with constant average degree, thereby extending the work of Coja-Oghlan and others. Finally, we investigate the behavior of the tensor join when applied to sparse random hypergraphs, a field previously unexplored in the literature.

The Imaging Near the Sun with Integrated Spectroscopy and Interferometry (INSIST) instrument, scheduled for the Parker Solar Probe's second suite of payloads, is engineered to capture solar images across a broad spectrum of wavelengths. By utilizing the Sun as an extended interferometer, it offers interferometric data to probe solar structures and magnetic fields. This study evaluates INSIST's performance across various imaging scenarios, including direct sunlight observations, coronal imaging, and interferometry. Results indicate that the coronal image resolution reaches approximately 1 milliarcsecond (mas) with signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 1000, while interferometric capabilities extend to 10 mas resolution down to fringe contrast levels of 1 percent. Crucially, the imaging fidelity of INSIST surpasses that of the Hubble Space Telescope by a factor of 100 in both spatial resolution and achievable fringe contrast.

This paper introduces a novel approach for analyzing continuous outcomes in clinical trials using longitudinal data modeled with natural cubic splines. By leveraging smoothness in the longitudinal trajectory, the method generates efficient estimators for treatment effects. The authors propose two constrained longitudinal analyses (CLAs) to ensure the consistency between the assumed smooth function and the estimated treatment interaction over time. The first constraint enforces a non-overlap condition on estimated treatment-smooth curves, mandating distinct potential outcome trajectories for treated and control groups at baseline. The second constraint restricts the overlap to the pooled data from both arms rather than separating them by treatment status. Simulation results indicate that the spline-based CLA methods yield more precise treatment effect estimates than standard two-sample $t$-tests, particularly when sample sizes are small. Additionally, applying this CLA framework to data from the Children's Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study (CADCS) offers valuable insights into Alzheimer's disease progression.

Reaction pathways in molecular simulations are frequently trapped in local minima during standard sampling, hindering the discovery of optimal routes. Conformational Space Annealing (CSA) addresses this challenge by integrating simulated annealing with a genetic algorithm to efficiently explore the conformational landscape. This approach was tested on the catalytic mechanism of the reaction between 1,3,5-trioxane and water catalyzed by hydronium ions. CSA successfully identified a pathway with a lower free energy barrier compared to previous findings, a result validated by comparison to a classical path derived via string methods. Furthermore, CSA enhanced the sampling of transition states, yielding more accurate estimates of activation entropy and enabling the derivation of an improved free energy landscape.

Church encodings represent a specific subset of simply typed lambda-calculus terms that model abstract data types, such as booleans, lists, and natural numbers. This paper investigates the impact of Church encodings on the computational expressivity of simply typed lambda-calculus. We introduce a new paradigm for computational expressivity grounded in reduction strategies, specifically examining how these encodings interact with such strategies. Our findings demonstrate that the inclusion of Church encodings can significantly heighten the expressivity of simply typed lambda-calculus.

This study investigates the novel derivatives of Lions type acting on measure functions, as well as their associated "measure Itô's formula." We establish the connection between a "measure Itô's formula" and the classical one, deriving an integral representation for the Lions derivative of an integral operator. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing the regularity of solutions to certain stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and, based on this, provide a "measure Itô's formula" for solutions to SDEs. Finally, we present a novel application of these equations to the analysis of mean-field control problems.

This paper demonstrates the application of topological tools, leveraging established results on separation axioms and compactness within the context of normal subgroups under hull-kernel topology. These techniques facilitate new insights into the structural properties of such subgroups equipped topologically.

This paper introduces a lightweight framework designed to enhance execution precision in database-driven neural networks without relying on specific data sets. By employing a data-driven approach, the study analyzes how varying data distributions impact network performance and subsequently proposes a pruning strategy that eliminates sensitive weights. These sensitive neurons are identified through a robustness metric that measures sensitivity to perturbations within the input space. Experimental results demonstrate that the resulting pruned network maintains nearly identical accuracy compared to its full counterpart even when database contents are concealed, and it exhibits significantly better generalization on unseen data. Furthermore, the framework effectively reduces model size while sustaining high accuracy, offering a viable solution for protecting sensitive information within neural networks.

This study introduces a prediction-based collision avoidance strategy for multi-robot formations. By integrating the error of motion predictions into the Time-Varying Artificial Potential Field (APF), the approach leverages prediction data to refine the potential field calculation. Specifically, incorporating prediction errors enhances collision avoidance capabilities and ensures that formations remain intact during maneuvers. Furthermore, theoretical analysis confirms the method's ability to prevent collisions and maintain structural integrity. Simulation results validate these conclusions, demonstrating an effective collision avoidance strategy that preserves formation coherence.

We present new observations of the Andromeda dwarf satellite Andromeda XXV (also designated And I) obtained with the Keck/DEMOSS instrument. These data allow us to determine the galaxy's mean line-of-sight stellar velocity dispersion ($\sigma_{0}$) of $10.2 \pm 0.4$ km s$^{-1}$ and its mean proper motion ($\mu_{0}$) of $0.11 \pm 0.01$ mas yr$^{-1}$. Utilizing these kinematic measurements, we calculate a mass-to-light ratio ($M/L$) of $1.9 \pm 0.4$ for And I, which is notably lower than the typical values found in other dwarf spheroidal galaxies. Additionally, we examine the stellar velocity anisotropy profile, finding that it is consistent with isotropy ($\beta = 0.1 \pm 0.2$). This result implies that And I is not a genuine dwarf spheroidal but rather a stellar streamlet resulting from the tidal disruption of a larger progenitor system.

This study introduces a new approach to uplink grant-free access that utilizes non-orthogonal sequences derived from a novel class of polyphase codes. These codes generate sequence sets characterized by low cross-correlations, which significantly enhance the system's ability to separate users. Performance is further improved through a Maximum Likelihood detector designed to account for interference between consecutive symbols. Simulation results indicate a substantial improvement in success probability for the proposed detector compared to existing methods. Additionally, Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that systems utilizing polyphase code-based non-orthogonal sequences achieve a notable boost in success probability and a substantial reduction in latency compared to conventional systems that rely on standard spreading sequences.

The research investigates consistent approximations for adiabatic dynamics in moist air, specifically focusing on how to address saturation and condensation. It demonstrates that the consistent constant $\kappa$ approximation, which yields linear dry adiabats and a piecewise linear potential temperature profile for moist adiabats, is derived by applying the exact moist adiabatic gradient formula across saturated and unsaturated regions. This exact formula accounts for the thermodynamic properties of dry air, water vapor, and condensed liquid water. Furthermore, it establishes that the consistent constant $\kappa$ approximation is the unique solution satisfying continuity in potential temperature and the conservation of moist static energy. Consequently, this uniqueness allows for the derivation of alternative approximations, such as the piecewise constant and piecewise linear approaches, by utilizing linear regression on specific thermodynamic variables. Additionally, it is shown that employing piecewise linear approximations for moist adiabats that remain piecewise linear for dry adiabats is impossible. Finally, numerical simulations of moist convection in 1-D and 2-D models illustrate that the consistent constant $\kappa$ approximation is superior to other methods, offering more realistic simulations of moist convective processes.

We establish that the exterior algebra corresponding to $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ algeba on a finite collection of elements forms a matroid. This result entails a matroidal characterization of the alternating tensor algebra for $\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm}$ as well. This analysis yields combinatorial insights into the matroid structure of $T_{alt}(\mathbb{F}_1^{\pm})$ and demonstrates that the matroid associated with the matroidal representation of the alternating tensor ring is isomorphic to the direct sum of the underlying matroids, which are themselves summed over the set of all subsets of the elements.

Dialogue state tracking (DS) is a crucial component of task-oriented speech understanding systems, yet current approaches often rely on manual feature engineering or struggle with limited training data. This study introduces a novel neural architecture for DS tracking that leverages an attentional confusion network (CN) encoder to synthesize predictions from multiple base models into a consolidated output. By using the attentional mechanism to selectively focus on significant base model predictions, the proposed method effectively filters out noise and enhances performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach achieves superior accuracy across all datasets, with improvements of 3.1\%, 3.2\%, and 3.1\% respectively for the MultiWOH 2.0 (Amazon), MultiWOH 2.0 (Google), and ALI datasets compared to a standard model using the base method. Furthermore, a hybrid model combining the proposed method with the attentional mechanism yields an additional gain of 3.3\% on the Amazon dataset, 3.4\% on the Google dataset, and 3.5\% on the ALI dataset.

The notion of regularised sums, previously utilized in the context of the Drinfeld moduli space of rank 2 vector bundles with degree zero and Theorem 1.2.1 in [1.2.1] (or more generally, in [1.2.1]), is now employed to define invariants for the moduli space of stable parabolic vector bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$. Specifically, this approach calculates the $q$-deformed invariants for $F_4$ and $G_2$ Kac-Moody groups in the case of rank 2 bundles with degree zero and regularized traces. This method extends to the computation of $q$-deformed invariants for all simple Lie groups in the case of regularized traces of moduli spaces of stable parabolic bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$.

In access structure theory, the qualified subsets are those authorized to act on behalf of a group, while universal access structures (UAS) represent a class where any combination of qualified subsets can be realized by any triple of subsets. This study focuses on asymptotically optimal UAS, defined by a complexity measure for 'n' minimal qualified subsets that grows at a rate of $\Theta(n)$. We demonstrate that the information theoretic lower bound of $n/2$ bits applies to all optimal UAS, and we further establish that there exist constructions achieving this bound up to an additive logarithmic term.

We introduce a method for evaluating diverse noise models and decoherence-induced estimators for entangled systems. This approach utilizes optimal estimators to determine the fidelity between ideal noiseless quantum states and their noisy counterparts. By employing this technique, we can effectively benchmark quantum states generated from various noise sources. Additionally, we demonstrate that our method offers a significant advantage over current practices by reducing the necessary measurement settings.

The paper presents a theoretical investigation into the origin of palm tree modes (PTMs) in tokamaks, which are characterized by a multi-peaked structure localized at the edge. The study demonstrates that these modes arise from the coalescence of multiple edge-localized modes (LEM s) at the onset of turbulence, occurring when magnetic islands merge. This phenomenon is explained through the nonlinear interaction between the primary mode and sidebands, which are identified as the fundamental components of the associated turbulent fluctuations. The work further elucidates the mechanism of sideband generation by analyzing the nonlinear coupling between the primary mode and the mode responsible for the turbulence. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive explanation for the formation of PTMs and their characteristic multi-peaked profile.

This study investigates the efficacy of pretrained models in accelerating the training of Neuron Nearest Mean Classifiers (NNC) for solving Continual Learning (CL) problems. Our approach involves freezing the pretrained model and computing Neuron Nearest Mean Classifiers for each task using the model's layer neurons. We demonstrate that pretrained models significantly enhance NNC performance, enabling it to outperform current state-of-the-art (SoTA) CL methods. Furthermore, we find that freezing only a few pretrained layers yields performance comparable to fully frozen SoTA methods. Additionally, our method substantially reduces the computational cost of training the classifier and updating memory, making it highly efficient. Finally, we show that NNC trained with pretrained models exhibits greater robustness to catastrophic forgetting than other SoTA techniques.

Most automated hate speech detection systems rely primarily on linguistic cues within the target text, often overlooking crucial socio-cultural context necessary for accurate analysis. This study introduces a new approach to integrating that contextual depth by leveraging multi-lingual social media discussions regarding specific events. We implemented this through a set of targeted queries designed to gather relevant contextual data for given targets. To integrate this information effectively, we developed a novel weighting mechanism that dynamically adjusts contextual importance based on the frequency of key phrases. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly boosts performance across various languages and target groups when compared to strong baseline models.

This study investigates how gap junction heterogeneity influences the synchronization of oscillatory neurons within networks organized into small-world (SW) and regular ring structures. We examine the impact of varying the width of degree distributions, alongside changes in coupling strength and connectivity. Results indicate that collective oscillations in heterogeneous networks are more resilient to fluctuations in coupling strength and initial conditions compared to homogeneous counterparts. Furthermore, increasing the width of degree distributions tends to synchronize the entire network, though this effect is contingent upon specific parameter values. In SW networks, collective oscillations are suppressed when the heterogeneity of high-degree (hub) nodes surpasses a specific threshold. Conversely, random destruction of nodes leads to the emergence of collective oscillations in previously synchronized homogeneous networks, a phenomenon also observed in heterogeneously connected networks.

We introduce a new strategy for debugging that generates repair suggestions by creating samples from a distribution of bugs and their corresponding fixes learned via deep neural networks. During initial evaluations on 1,000 randomly selected issues from the OpenJDK repository, 20% of the detected bugs matched human repairs exactly. Additionally, 50% of the suggestions included valid repairs alongside extra content. Our approach also demonstrated higher performance than existing state-of-the-art methods across 40% of the cases, with all valid system-generated corrections being discovered prior to human identification. Finally, we conducted a study with 20 participants to assess the practical usability of this technique, yielding promising results.

This study introduces a generalized superposition inner bound for arbitrary broadcast and multiple-access broadcast channels, extending the capabilities developed by Csiszár and Körner in their seminal 1971 and 1973 works. The proposed framework leverages interference architecture to derive tighter inner bounds. Specifically, we present a four-step generalization of the binning technique. First, we employ binning to generate a broadcast channel model featuring a degraded interference structure akin to the deterministic model analyzed in their earlier papers. Second, we extend this model to include random interference. Third, we apply superposition coding to a broadcast channel where receivers decode messages based on degradedness. Finally, we generalize this degraded broadcast channel into one affected by interference. The inner bounds developed in this paper encompass and generalize the achievable rate regions established in their original publications.
