Scoliosis management frequently depends on precise imaging to track disease progression and assess surgical outcomes. Although robotic ultrasound offers a cost-effective alternative to conventional methods, its diagnostic accuracy remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the reliability of robotic ultrasound in measuring spinous process angles for determining scoliosis curve magnitude. We recruited 20 adolescent idiopathic scoliosis patients and had a trained radiologist obtain baseline X-rays for reference. Subsequently, a trained clinician acquired ultrasound images of the same patients twice, with a four-week interval between sessions. The radiologist then measured the scoliosis angles from these images. Inter- and intra-observer reliability were quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), while Bland-Altman plots analyzed systematic and random errors. The robotic ultrasound demonstrated excellent reliability for measuring scoliosis curves (ICC = 0.96). Furthermore, the random error was negligible (0.2°), and the mean systematic bias was minimal (0.1°). These findings indicate that robotic ultrasound is a trustworthy method for quantifying curves in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.

This study introduces a new approach for duration modeling that allows for the identification of distinct segments within the duration distribution, contrasting with traditional methods that rely on a single, continuous form. The proposed algorithm is designed to be robust against outliers and incorporates a straightforward penalty for excessive segment creation to prevent overfitting. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through analysis of both simulated data and real-world examples, including the well-known "hump-shaped" distribution observed in marriage durations.

This study examines the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) to detect hate speech within the provided dataset. We evaluated three methodologies: a rule-based approach, a supervised machine learning model, and a deep learning system. The results indicate that the deep learning solution yielded the highest performance, achieving an accuracy of 90.21% alongside a precision of 90.11%.

This work introduces an improved version of the Multi-Instrument Mixed-Object Modeling (MIMO) framework, termed MiniMIMO. The primary advancement is a new unmixing procedure designed to resolve the limitation in original MIMO where inactive subnetworks contribute no useful information. By unmixing the input data prior to subnetwork processing, the method ensures all subnetworks handle mixed signals, thereby enhancing their contribution to final predictions. Additionally, the model incorporates a novel loss function to encourage the learning of an improved demixing matrix. Empirical evaluations on a public dataset confirm MiniMIMO's superior performance over both the standard MIMO and conventional deep learning baselines.

Historical document analysis is a complex and often difficult endeavor, primarily because locating suitable datasets is challenging. While many such documents are available in digital formats, they frequently suffer from noise, rendering them unsuitable for direct use in training machine learning models. This study introduces a novel document restoration pipeline designed to clean historical texts by addressing common artifacts such as holes, stains, and ink smudges. We evaluate the proposed approach on the "Hole and Stain Removal" task using the historical "Hole and Stain Removal" dataset. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing solutions, achieving a higher PSNR of 26.59 and a greater SSIM of 0.8199. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these restored documents yield superior classification accuracy when applied to the "Hole and Stain Removal" dataset.

The low stiffness of compliant industrial robots often results in trajectory inaccuracies, prompting this study to enhance their tracking precision through the application of a nonlinear disturbance observer (NDOO). The implementation strategy involves a position feedback control loop integrating the Nonlinear Disturbance Observer with a Nonlinear Sliding Mode Controller (S-MPC). The NDOO is designed to estimate and observe the total disturbances affecting the robot, while the S-MPC generates the requisite control signals. The effectiveness of this approach was validated through experiments comparing a standard Nonlinear Sliding Mode Controller against the proposed S-MPDO-S-MPC hybrid system. Results indicate that the proposed method significantly improves trajectory accuracy, reducing the tracking error by 30.4% and 24.9% along the x and y axes, respectively.

Myocardial infarction (MI) is a leading cause of death and disability, often resulting in lasting health issues. While recent research has utilized electronic health records (EHRs) to map the long-term health trajectory following MI, this study specifically investigates how sex and ethnicity influence these outcomes. We introduce a novel framework combining clustering and causal inference to identify ethnicity- and sex-specific patterns of long-term conditions (CLTs) linked to MI. Our analysis of EHR data from 10,000 MI patients reveals that clustering uncovers distinct CLT profiles across different sexes and ethnicities. Furthermore, causal inference techniques demonstrate that both sex and ethnicity are associated with altered probabilities of developing these long-term conditions after an MI.

A new adaptation of Becke's multipole scheme is introduced to efficiently calculate couplings between bound electronic states and the electronic continuum. This modification significantly improves the convergence of multipole expansions for continuum-based integrals by incorporating radial functions asymptotic behavior at large distances. Testing against a model Hamiltonian demonstrates that achieving the same accuracy now demands a much shorter multipole expansion, resulting in a substantial reduction in the overall computational cost for calculating continuum bound-state interactions.

The Metric Dimension problem involves determining the smallest subset of vertices in a graph $G$ capable of uniquely identifying all other vertices through distinct distance vectors, known as a resolving set. This study examines the computational complexity of the problem when parameterized by various graph metrics and structural features. We demonstrate that it remains W(1)-hard when parameterized by pathwidth and dual parameterized by distance to a path forest. Conversely, it is fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) when parameterized by treewidth, distance to a path forest, distance to a bipartite graph, distance to a split graph, distance to a threshold graph, or distance to a co-bipartite graph. Additionally, the problem is solvable in polynomial time if parameterized by distance to a cactus graph.

For a directed space defined as a dcpo equipped with the Scott topology, the upper, lower, and convex powerdomains are all directed spaces. In contrast, this property does not extend to directed spaces when employing alternative topologies. This paper investigates directed sets endowed with the finite complement topology, the topology of finite complements, and the co-finite topology, determining which of these structures yield powerdomains that retain the qualities of directed spaces.

This study examines how a low-latitude radiative heating source in the lower troposphere influences the global climate of a "hothouse" Earth. Utilizing a 1.5-dimensional climate model, we find that this heating mechanism suppresses cloud cover and diminishes precipitation, particularly in the low latitudes. Additionally, it intensifies lower-atmospheric warming and amplifies meridional heat transport. These outcomes are driven by a shift in convection from a moist-adiabatic ascent to a dry-adiabatic rise, which alters the vertical temperature structure and the distribution of water vapor. The findings underscore the critical importance of accurately modeling the vertical distribution of solar absorption and long-wave emission for both modern and ancient planetary climates.

We introduce a covariant higher-spin Yang-Mills theory operating within anti-de Sitter space, formulated as an action dependent on the curvatures of associated field strengths. This framework constitutes an anti-de Sitter extension of the flat-space higher-spin Yang-Mills concept originally proposed by Fradkin and Volovich. Notably, the resulting action manifests as a sum of gauge-invariant terms, each being of higher-derivative order. In the limit where the anti-de Sitter curvature approaches zero, our derivation reproduces the established flat-space action.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly prevalent in real-world applications, yet the massive datasets used to train them often contain significant noise. This label noise severely hampers DNN performance, and while existing correction methods exist, they typically rely on rule-based approaches that are rigid and fail to address the diverse origins of noise. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Bayesian statistics-guided Label Refurbishment Mechanism (BLRM), an innovative approach that operates under a Bayesian framework. The method utilizes a teacher-student architecture where the teacher network, trained via Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, generates probability distributions for training data. By analyzing these distributions, BLRM identifies clean labels and estimates the source of noisy ones, thereby refining network accuracy. Empirical results demonstrate that BLRM surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques on three major benchmark datasets—CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and FashionMNIST—across varying levels of noise intensity.

This paper investigates the existence of regular simplexes within the unit cube $Q_n$ and demonstrates that a nondegenerate regular simplex can only be found when the number of interpolation nodes $N$ meets the condition $N \geq n+1$. Furthermore, we present constructions of full-dimensional regular simplexes for the cases $N=n$ and $N=n+1$. For the boundary case where $N=n$, although these simplexes are regular, they are not contained within the unit cube $Q_n$.

This paper introduces a novel approach to determine the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix for a specific type of Markov chain defined on an infinite state space. The authors leverage techniques from complex analysis to yield a closed-form formula for this polynomial. Furthermore, the study provides a method to calculate the zeros of the resulting rational function, which correspond to the eigenvalues, and evaluates their multiplicity. These results are then applied to the context of a correlated random walk, where the random step size is determined by the most recent movement direction.

We introduce a set of proof transformations designed to streamline termination arguments that employ our proposed clock-based mechanism. By strategically decreasing the use of the clock within every function definition, these simplifications can potentially make proofs more accessible. Our approach consists of two core transformations that are governed by specific patterns in how clocks are utilized. To facilitate these, we present a denotational semantics for our system and utilize it to establish the correctness of the transformations through a proof of their soundness.

Simulating wall-bounded flows remains a significant challenge in computational fluid dynamics. A key component of these models is the hairpin packet, a coherent structure that has been extensively studied through direct numerical simulations (DNS) and large-eddy simulations (LES). This paper examines the impact of the initial condition used to generate these packets on DNS and analyzes the resulting turbulent kinetic energy spectra. Additionally, the study compares these DNS outcomes against LES results, demonstrating that the initial condition significantly affects the spectra and the degree of agreement between DNS and LES. The paper further shows that while spectral agglomeration can improve the accuracy of LES, the initial condition still plays a critical role in the quality of this spectral agglomeration.

The baby Skyrme model features two distinct soliton solutions characterized by either semicircular or square profiles. Its gauged variant, incorporating a topological mass term, introduces a third profile resembling a flattened disk. This study investigates the properties of such topological solitons within a background defined by non-abelian gauge fields. The analysis reveals that while solitons with square cross-sections maintain their topological charge under any gauge background, those built from semi-circular or disk-like profiles may experience charge dissociation or annihilation. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that circular solitons exhibit higher stability compared to their square counterparts when subjected to strong gauge field backgrounds.

This work examines the low-energy physics of a three-dimensional lattice model featuring Weyl nodes located at opposite corners of the Brillouin zone. We employ a bond-dependent, directional hopping model to capture the chiral anomaly inherent to Weyl fermions. Our analysis demonstrates that crystal symmetry dictates the system's phases, which encompass metallic, insulating, and superconducting states. Furthermore, we identify a unique nematic superconducting phase characterized by broken rotational symmetry, arising from the specific form of the hopping term. Finally, we outline the phase diagram and discuss the transitions between these states.

Optical nanoantennas serve as a versatile platform for manipulating light at the sub-wavelength scale, a capability that is often constrained by the difficulty of independently tailoring their optical responses. In this study, we demonstrate an adaptable design for a dual-port bowtie antenna, wherein spectral resonances are independently positioned in the transmission spectra of each port. This outcome is achieved by introducing an asymmetry in the gap between the antenna's arms. Furthermore, we analyze light propagation through this structure using a coupled mode theory framework. The proposed design offers significant potential for applications such as advanced sensing technologies and the development of multi-channel filters.

While plastic events in amorphous materials are often likened to plasticity in ordered crystals, a key distinction lies in the fact that amorphous systems lack a well-defined thermodynamic state. This absence of a thermodynamic framework complicates the description of their mechanical behavior. To address this, a phenomenological model is proposed that effectively captures the mechanical response of a simple amorphous system. The model's validity is demonstrated through results from a standard energy landscape simulation, which features a single parameter: the magnitude of energy dissipated during each plastic event. Furthermore, the proposed framework is applied to analyze the mechanical response of a simple shear simulation, revealing that its predictions align closely with the simulation data.

This study investigates silicene decorated by manganese (Mn) atoms, specifically examining how the position of Mn affects the onsite Hubbard interaction ($U$) and the effective mass of carriers. Our findings indicate that the value of $U$ is position-dependent: when Mn is placed at a topoh site, $U$ increases, whereas placement at an hollowsite causes it to decrease. Furthermore, we observe that placing Mn at the topoh site reduces the effective mass of electrons and holes, while the hollow-site configuration increases it. These observations are explained through an analysis of Mn's $d$-orbitals and silicene's $\pi$-band structure. Finally, we analyze the stability of this decorated silicene using first-principles calculations.

The Galactic Centre supernova remnant Sgr A East is widely believed to be the aftermath of a supernova explosion that occurred within the central parsec of our Galaxy. This study presents new observations from the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, which reveal a 1.2σ excess in the hard X-ray band (10–100 keV) from the region surrounding Sgr A East. This excess flux is likely attributable to the supernova remnant itself, though a systematic error could also explain the finding. Assuming the emission originates from the remnant, we find that the hard X-ray flux is comparable to that of the Crab Nebula. By applying a synchrotron model, we determine that the supernova explosion took place approximately 1.5 parsecs from the Galactic Centre. This finding supports the hypothesis that the progenitor star was a massive star that orbited within the central parsec before its demise.

Class imbalance is a prevalent challenge in data analysis, particularly within machine learning. This study examines the performance impacts of unequal class distributions on K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Support Vector Machines (SVM) algorithms, comparing their results to the well-documented literature on neural networks. Specifically, we evaluate the efficacy of various techniques to mitigate imbalance effects on these algorithms using the KDD CUP 1999 dataset. Our findings indicate that, similar to neural networks, SVM and KNN are vulnerable to class imbalance; however, SVM tends to be more susceptible than KNN. Additionally, resampling methods prove more effective than other approaches in reducing performance degradation for SVM and KNN, with SMOTE emerging as the superior strategy for both algorithms.

This study examines how U.S. local news outlets covered COVID-19 by analyzing their reporting volume, content, and tone through a lens of political and geographic influences. We evaluated coverage across 1,000 news sources, representing approximately 90% of outlets with a news division, utilizing a representative sample of 1,000 stories from each source. Our findings indicate that while political affiliation and geographic location significantly shaped the frequency and substance of reporting, the local news environment played a more pivotal role in shaping the tone of those stories.

This study introduces a hybrid Fast Multipole Method (FMM) designed for modern multicore architectures, leveraging both shared and distributed memory to achieve superior computational efficiency. Designed to maximize the advantages of next-generation supercomputers, this approach combines the distributed-memory FMM (DM-FMM) with the shared-memory variant (SM-FMM). Specifically, it utilizes SM-FMM to handle local clusters of particles within individual processes and extends the FMM tree across multiple processes to model interactions between them. By employing a novel communication strategy, particle data is transmitted between processes with a single network round-trip, thereby significantly reducing latency. Furthermore, an optimized data layout minimizes network bandwidth consumption and enhances scalability. Benchmarking results across the BlueGene/Q supercomputer at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC) demonstrate that this hybrid FMM outperforms existing solutions by a factor of 2.5, while maintaining excellent parallel scalability. These capabilities make the method highly suitable for demanding, large-scale astrophysical simulations.

The JLab Hall A collaboration has conducted a comprehensive measurement of the double-spin asymmetry for the $ep \to ep$ elastic scattering process, utilizing a proton beam with a longitudinal polarization of approximately 30% at an incident energy of 1.1 GeV. Data were collected across a range of momentum transfers ($Q^2$) from 0.2 to 0.45 $ \mathrm{ GeV}^2 $ and at four distinct values of the electron scattering angle. The resulting asymmetries are compared against predictions from various models of nucleon form factors and response functions. The findings reveal a strong correlation between the measured asymmetries and the ratio of the neutron to proton form factors, $ G_E^N/G_M^N $. Additionally, the study provides a detailed uncertainty analysis, which is critical for future investigations into the neutron-to-proton form factors ratio.

Behavioral cloning, a supervised learning technique, has recently been successfully applied to high-degrees-of-freedom control tasks. However, a significant challenge remains: aligning the actions of a student policy with those of an expert when they operate under different policy representations. This paper introduces a novel approach termed "augmented policy cloning," which incorporates domain adaptation to facilitate the transfer of behavior from expert to student representations. The method functions by training a domain translation policy that maps the student's policy representation into the domain of the expert. We demonstrate that this strategy effectively learns precise, hard-to-control movements, such as complex ballet steps, when transferring from motion capture data to a robotic quadruped.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 36 fb$^{-1}$ from the LHC, this study investigates the associated production of a neutral heavy scalar or pseudoscalar ($H$ or $A$) and a Standard Model Higgs boson via top-quark fusion. The search, which targets the decay mode where the heavy resonance decays into a $Z$ boson and the SM Higgs decays into two bottom quarks ($t\bar{t} \to t\bar{t} \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH \to bWH

This study presents a digital signal processing approach for analyzing the output of a resonant spin maser, specifically a diamond nitrogen-vacancy center maser operating at room temperature. We implemented a baseband up-conversion method using a direct quadrature modulation scheme to digitally process maser signals. Our results demonstrate that this technique enhances the signal-to-noise ratio by a factor of 1.41 compared to standard detection methods. Furthermore, we evaluated the up-conversion scheme's ability to accurately recover maser parameters, including Larmor frequency, relaxation time, and magnetic field strength. Ultimately, this method offers a viable pathway for integrating high-performance spin maser systems with modern digital processing architectures.

We present a new method for constructing examples of K3 surface automorphisms with specific dynamical characteristics by employing hypergeometric groups. This approach leverages the elliptic fibrations inherent in these groups to generate an automorphism with a specified dynamical behavior on each fiber.

We investigate the decay of a visible sector neutralino into a hidden sector neutralino and a high-energy gamma ray, proposing its detection via the internal conversion of these gamma rays into pairs of charged particles within the electric fields of atomic nuclei. This conversion mechanism results in distinctive, narrow, back-to-back tracks that are precisely collimated. We identify three viable scenarios for the hidden sector: a real scalar, an imaginary pseudoscalar, or a fermionic state. We calculate the branching ratios for these decays and determine the resulting pair production rates per collider event. Furthermore, we outline strategies for identifying these signals amidst detector backgrounds and assess the collider's potential sensitivity to these specific decays.

Graphs naturally map to topological spaces, where the genus of a specific graph is defined as the smallest possible genus of a surface that can embed it. This paper investigates the relationship between a graph's genus and the properties of its subgraphs, with a focus on subgraphs that are maximal with respect to edge inclusion. We introduce the concept of the "genus spectrum," which represents the set of genera found among all edge-maximal subgraphs of a given graph. Our findings establish that the genus spectrum of any graph with genus $g$ always includes the value $g$ itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a graph with genus $g$, the genus spectrum necessarily contains all integers from $g$ down to $g - \lfloor\frac{g}{2}\rfloor + 1$.

This study introduces a novel, fully decentralized, variance-reduced stochastic optimization approach for convex objectives, engineered to minimize communication rounds and enhance robustness against adversarial noise. The method's name, ADMM-Var, is derived from its adaptation of the well-known ADMM framework, which leverages message passing to facilitate round-efficient, fully distributed learning. By integrating variance reduction techniques, ADMM-Var achieves a communication complexity of $O(1/\epsilon)$ for a target accuracy of $\epsilon$, a significant improvement over the standard ADMM's $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ complexity requiring $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ communication rounds to reach the same precision. The algorithm maintains performance despite the presence of adversarial noise within the message passing mechanism. Furthermore, the method supports implementation across heterogeneous nodes, capable of accommodating non-identical local objectives.

A new approach to training language models for low-resource settings is introduced by leveraging the semantic representations from established high-resource languages through transfer learning. Building on BERT, this methodology involves pre-training a model using shared-ancestry languages to learn common semantics, which is then fine-tuned with limited data from the target language. Experimental results indicate that this transfer learning strategy significantly outperforms training from scratch, particularly when fine-tuning on a high-resource related language. Furthermore, this work offers a cost-effective and efficient framework for developing multilingual BERT variants.

Gas Time Projection Chambers (GTPCs) serve as a versatile platform for dark matter detection, yet a significant hurdle remains in distinguishing electron recoils (ER) from nuclear recoils (R). While current GTPC systems rely on pulse height analysis in a single plane, this study introduces new discrimination observables leveraging the GTPC's 3-dimensional geometry. These new metrics analyze the spatial distribution of ER signals versus nuclear recoil tracks, achieving ER/RR classification efficiencies of 99.9% and 80%, respectively, with an electronic noise rejection factor exceeding 100. This performance surpasses traditional single-plane methods, which typically offer only 99% ER and 60% RR efficiencies. Consequently, the proposed new observables enhance the GTPC's utility for detecting WIMPs, allowing for a nuclear recoil exposure limit 100 times lower than that achievable with single-plane discrimination.

We introduce a deep learning framework designed to assess driver behaviors by integrating expert knowledge regarding how drivers respond to external driving conditions. While current methods typically rely on rule-based systems that are difficult to construct and maintain due to the complexity of defining behaviors, our approach leverages the domain expertise of traffic psychologists to assess the alignment between driver actions and environmental factors. By extracting this knowledge into a rule-driven deep learning model, our system enhances the assessment of driver behaviors. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating expert insights through our proposed method improves assessment accuracy by 10% compared to models without such integration.

Although scene text recognition has seen significant recent advancements, the field remains hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality datasets. This paper introduces the Open-Vocabulary (OpenVV) dataset, a pioneering resource designed to address the limitations of existing data. Unlike prior efforts, the dataset is continuously updated to incorporate text on objects never previously seen, thereby simulating the real-world challenge of encountering diverse vocabulary. Collected from over 100,001 Google image search results, the dataset comprises more than 100,001 image-text pairs. To ensure balanced representation, the collection includes rare languages such as Chinese, German, and Japanese, alongside English. Furthermore, the dataset undergoes rigorous quality assurance to filter out noisy labels. To maximize its utility, the paper also presents a comprehensive data augmentation strategy that significantly improves the robustness of scene text recognition architectures. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that models trained on the OpenVV dataset achieve superior performance compared to those trained on prior benchmarks, highlighting the dataset's effectiveness in enhancing such models.

We propose a novel metric to quantify the similarity between two random fields defined under different regimes. This approach involves calculating the mutual information between the fields after projecting them onto an optimally chosen orthonormal basis. The framework is demonstrated by analyzing the Ising model in the presence of a magnetic field, contrasting its behavior between the high-temperature and critical regions.

The dynamics are modeled using the dimensionless Darcy-Brinkman-Maxwell equations, which reduce to the dimensionless Navier-Stokes equations in the limit of high magnetic Reynolds numbers. The primary objective is to determine the stability of the levitated object by analyzing the eigenvalues of the linearized system around a steady state. The results indicate that magnetic levitation significantly influences the initial perturbations, thereby affecting the stability of the levitated object. The analysis further reveals that the eigenvalues of the linearized system exhibit a notable shift in magnitude compared to those of the non-levitated case, suggesting that magnetic levitation plays a crucial role in determining the stability of the levitated object. We demonstrate that the Hecke L-functions associated with primitive elements for SL2(Z) exhibit behavior that is nearly optimal relative to the Riemann Hypothesis, with coefficients exhibiting statistical distributions closely resembling those of cuspidal Hecke eigenforms for Spn(Z).

We have developed a method to calculate transport metrics within junctions comprising normal conductors and graphene. This approach relies on the Green's function technique combined with the tight-binding approximation for the electronic structure, distinguishing itself by accounting for the disparities in electronic structure at the interfaces of connected systems. The validity of our methodology is confirmed by benchmarking it against full numerical simulations. Furthermore, we apply this framework to examine transport within graphene-based point contacts, specifically analyzing armchair nanoribbon contacts paired with lead atoms.

This work examines the ergodic means derived from a monotone operator that is weakly nonlinear within a Banach lattice under conditions ensuring convergence in both weak and norm terms within that space. These findings are subsequently utilized to establish ergodic representations applicable to nonexpansive mappings defined on closed, bounded, and invariant subsets of the lattice, as well as to derive corresponding mean ergodic theorems for mappings that are weakly nonexpansive.

The initial conditions of a quark-gluon plasma are pivotal for modeling heavy-ion collisions. This study examines how variations in the medium's initial profile influence the pressure gradient and the flow velocity of generated light hadrons. We find that, regardless of initial configuration, light hadrons exhibit a transverse flow profile with a mean velocity of approximately 0.45c, which aligns with experimental observations. However, the initial medium profile significantly shapes the flow profile's curvature and the distribution of flow velocities. We propose that these characteristics of light-hadron flow can be utilized to infer the geometry of the QGP at the onset of the collision.

This study introduces a novel approach named SASK, which integrates sparse approximate optimal control with sparse kernel approximations to solve partial differential equations. By leveraging sparsity in the approximate solution of the dual problem, SALK significantly reduces computational costs associated with evaluating kernel matrix-vector products within the primal solution phase. Furthermore, the method employs sparse generalized Hessian approximation to accelerate dual optimization, rendering the overall process highly efficient. Numerical experiments on diverse partial differential equations demonstrate that SALK achieves superior performance compared to existing alternatives, delivering enhanced speed and effectiveness.

We present a resonance framework for modeling DC electric field interactions with water molecules, which is validated by fitting parameters to experimental ionization cross-sections from established literature. The derived resonance parameters align well with theoretical predictions and experimental data, with calculated values closely matching those in previous studies. This approach offers a robust method for constructing accurate potential models to simulate molecular ionization under varying electric field strengths.

The study examines the behavior of Sinkhorn algorithms in the context of Schrödinger problems where no solution exists. We demonstrate that such algorithms converge to a specific non-solution state, effectively acting as a Bregman projection onto a subspace containing all valid solutions. We also establish that these limit distributions are invariant under certain conditions, although they may not always exhibit uniqueness.

This study examines the top-quark pair production cross-section within quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at the center-of-mass energy of the LHC, utilizing a data set of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions with an integrated luminosity of 20.2 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector. The analysis focuses on events containing at least two isolated leptons of various flavors and significant missing transverse momentum, corresponding to the top-quark pair decay channel involving leptons. The measured cross-section is 8.71 ± 0.30 (stat.) ± 0.45 (sys.) mb, which aligns well with QCD predictions at both next-to-leading order and next-to-next-to-leading accuracy.

We investigate the entanglement dynamics of a disordered interacting spin system coupled to a central qubit or cavity mode. By combining a perturbative approach with a numerically exact solution of the master equation, we identify a regime where the entanglement between the central spin and the surrounding bath exhibits diffusive growth at long times. This behavior contrasts with the typical linear growth of entanglement observed in noninteracting systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the perturbative method yields results that closely match those obtained through exact solutions, thereby validating its utility for studying entanglement in such complex, interacting contexts.

The aim of this paper is to demonstrate that the generalized Bessel function exhibits Janaskovic convexity and starliness within the unit disk $|z|<1$, subject to certain constraints on the parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, and $\delta$. Furthermore, we derive bounds on these functions regarding their order of starliness and convexity based on the magnitude of $z|$.

The pandemic's impact on urban environments was profound, ranging from reduced physical activity and disrupted social interactions to the erosion of local economies and green spaces. While the immediate effects are well-documented, there is a critical need to understand the enduring consequences on urban encounters and community resilience. This study utilizes data from 1,000 participants across 20 neighborhoods in Zurich, Switzerland, to analyze changes in physical activity and encounter patterns before and during the pandemic. Findings indicate that pre-existing disparities in physical activity and social encounters were amplified post-pandemic, with some neighborhoods experiencing significantly more diverse encounter patterns than others. These results underscore the importance of urban design in fostering resilient communities capable of withstanding and recovering from future crises.

This study introduces a novel algorithm designed to address the fully coupled system of mass and energy balance equations within a one-dimensional slab model of the snowpack. Unlike traditional approaches, such as the Sequentially Implicit method, which decouple these equations, our method couples the mass balance with the fully implicit Solution of the Energy balance using the Finite Steps Snow Model (FSMSN). Within this framework, the snowpack is divided into multiple layers, with energy balance solved implicitly within each layer and mass balance solved explicitly at layer interfaces. The primary advantages of FSMSN are its numerical stability and its capacity to accurately simulate rapid transient events, such as rapid warming. The algorithm's performance was validated against FSMSN benchmark results and compared with a traditional Fully Implicit method. The analysis demonstrates that FSMSN achieves results comparable to the Fully Implicit method while requiring significantly fewer computational time steps.

This study investigates the interaction between chiral emitters and optical cavity modes, focusing on how cavity-induced modifications to the spontaneous emission rate depend on the emitter's handedness. We demonstrate that a single-handed optical cavity can selectively couple with only one specific polarized emitter type, thereby enhancing their interaction with light. This effect is achieved through an optical cavity constructed using a one-dimensional photonic crystal featuring a localized defect, with the structure's periodicity tapered to create handedness. Notably, the optical cavity exhibits a chiral resonance confined to circularly polarized left-handed light, which propagates exclusively in one direction. Consequently, chiral emitters whose dipole moments are oriented transversely and possess oscillation patterns matching the left-handed resonance experience a significant increase in spontaneous emission rates. In contrast, emitters with longitudinally oriented dipoles or those responsive to right-handed polarization remain uncoupled from the mode. Our findings indicate that chiral emitters with transition dipole moments aligned transversely to the cavity axis achieve the maximum enhancement of their spontaneous emission rates.

This conclusion is achieved by identifying the linear dilaton field and the Liouville field with the dual fields of the two copies of $AdS_2$ in the context of the string framework. Urban underground infrastructure systems (UGS) are vital to modern society, yet their complexity and interconnectivity make it difficult to assess how disruptions impact surface operations. While existing research has analyzed the interdependence of underground systems, there is a lack of focus on surface infrastructure's role in supporting them. The GUIDES (Ground Infrastructure Interdependency Decision-making Support) framework addresses this by creating a bidirectional mapping of urban underground and surface infrastructures. By integrating this bidirectional link into a multi-layered network model, the GUIDES approach facilitates the identification of critical underground systems and the evaluation of how surface disruptions affect subsurface operations. The primary goal of this research is to enhance decision-making capabilities for emergency responders and system operators.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) is a powerful technique for investigating local vibrational modes, offering sub-molecular spatial resolution. However, a persistent challenge remains: distinguishing between the chemical signature of a target sample and the chemical contributions arising from the metallic tip. This study demonstrates that the chemical effect is the dominant factor in the TERS spectra of gold nanoparticles, regardless of the specific tip material used. We further show that the tip's material plays a crucial role in determining the magnitude of the electromagnetic effect, yet this role is secondary when compared to the chemical effect. Consequently, our findings suggest that the chemical signal, rather than the electromagnetic one, primarily governs the observed tip-enhanced Raman spectra.

Spiral galaxies are expected to host Axion-Matter Interactions (AMIs), which could generate a distinct, large-scale matter distribution. This study utilizes the Dark Energy Survey's 1000 galaxy sample to conduct a comprehensive search for these AMI effects. The analysis employs a model-independent technique to eliminate systematic errors and applies a Gaussian Process model to filter out anisotropic foregrounds. The results indicate no evidence for AMI effects within the dataset. The paper further outlines the optimal conditions for detecting AMI signals in spiral galaxies, specifically a sample of approximately 1000 galaxies, a distance range of 100 to 300 Mpc, and a coupling strength $\alpha$ between $10^{-1}$ and $10^{-1}$. Finally, a detailed examination of the model's sensitivity to various assumptions regarding the underlying matter distribution is provided.

Ammonium sulfate ($\alpha$-$(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4$) serves as a prototypical ferroelectric material, undergoing a second-order phase transition from a paraelectric cubic phase to a monoclinic one at the Curie temperature ($T_C \approx 233$ K). This study employs Raman spectroscopy, dielectric measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to examine the phase transition and the associated entropy shift. The findings reveal that the transition is driven by the progressive ordering of ammonium ions, accompanied by softening of specific vibrational modes. The entropy reduction is primarily attributed to the diminishing configurational entropy of these ammonium ions as they order, rather than changes in solvent entropy. The study further elucidates a correlation linking the Curie temperature to the entropy of the ammonium ions' ordering.

Previous research indicates that individuals often struggle to avoid probability-matching when learning from the environment. Yet, the mechanisms behind this propensity and its relationship to avoidance learning remain unclear. We investigated this by examining how the environment's predictability influences probability-matching behavior and how such behavior impacts avoidance learning. Participants engaged in a task where they selected between two stimuli to earn rewards or prevent aversive outcomes. Our findings revealed that as environmental predictability decreased, participants' likelihood of probability-matching increased. Furthermore, those exhibiting higher levels of probability-matching showed greater difficulty avoiding negative outcomes, suggesting that suboptimal reward matching may impair the proper encoding of negative feedback. These results offer insight into the link between probability-matching and avoidance learning, potentially explaining why individuals fail to optimally steer clear of adverse situations.

The set of quantum states defined by specific sets of observables can be linked to other sets through local operations and classical communication (local operations and communication). This study examines the implications of such transformations for nonlocality and contextuality. We establish that the nonlocality and contextuality observed in one set of states are preserved by these mappings. Consequently, the transformations allow us to connect various nonlocality and contextuality frameworks, thereby extending the range of quantum resources available for research and experimentation.

We introduce a novel randomized algorithm for approximate near neighbor problems in Euclidean spaces, grounded in Lp distance metrics. This method utilizes preprocessing to establish an approximation factor of $\tilde{O}(k^{1/p})$ with a query time complexity of $\tilde{O}(d)$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality. Our approach subsumes and enhances existing techniques for both approximate nearest neighbor and approximate one-sided closest vector queries. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model inherently bypasses the longstanding dimension-dependent lower bounds for two-sided approximate near neighbor queries, specifically those established by Andoni et al. (STOC 2015) and Indyk and Woodruff (FOCS 2013).

This study introduces an iterative Bayesian unfolding method designed to address measurement errors in quantum computers, featuring cost scaling that is linear with respect to circuit depth. We demonstrate the technique's efficacy using noise simulations on random circuits, where it successfully recovers output probabilities across various noise models. Furthermore, the method accurately reconstructs probabilities for QAOA circuits subjected to different noise conditions, successfully restoring the original noise-free cost function landscape.

This study examines how users perceive and collaborate with robots when learning task-specific input mappings. We developed a task-oriented framework that enables robots to acquire user preferences for controlling movements and, consequently, to tailor their own motion plans. While initial interactions require multiple exchanges to fully learn these mappings, performance improves significantly as users become familiar with the robot. Our findings reveal a substantial positive impact on collaboration efficiency, highlighting a rapid learning curve where user effectiveness grows exponentially after just a few exchanges. Furthermore, we demonstrate that disclosing a robot's internal preferences for task-specific mappings to its human partner enhances user productivity.

This study introduces a novel representation for global navigation metrics termed HiTMap, designed to address global issues within hierarchical metric field representations. While preserving the advantages of global metric maps, such as precise local obstacle detection, HiTMap enables a more efficient and robust management of these maps through a multi-resolution hierarchical structure. Specifically, it facilitates the dynamic adjustment of planning and simulation goals based on the robot's current state, effectively balancing computational efficiency with necessary performance. Furthermore, the framework supports the incremental learning of these metrics from real-world robot experiences. Experimental results across both simulated environments and a physical robot demonstrate that the HiTMap approach achieves superior performance in global navigation tasks.

This study introduces a novel image reconstruction approach for Computed Tomography (CT) that integrates deep learning with the data fidelity framework. The proposed deep learning component is a fully convolutional encoder-decoder architecture designed to restore images from undersampled projections. This model is trained on data from multiple scanners, enabling it to generalize effectively to various scanner types and handling diverse noise characteristics such as photon starvation noise and ring artifacts. By incorporating the learned deep prior into the data fidelity term, the method successfully reconstructs high-quality images even from a limited number of projections. Experimental results demonstrate that the traditional back-projection technique fails to produce acceptable imagery under these conditions, whereas our approach yields visually superior images. Furthermore, the quantitative evaluation confirms that our proposed method outperforms conventional iterative algorithms.

We introduce a novel approach to predict light propagation through one-dimensional photonic bandgap structures, grounded in a non-local theory. This method utilizes an effective gap width that accounts for the finite slopes at interfaces, contrasting with traditional local models like the transfer-matrix approach which rely on effective refractive indices derived from the Bloch theorem. By incorporating the concept of effective gap width, the proposed model offers greater accuracy in predicting the positions of light resonance peaks within the bandgap compared to the standard transfer-matrix method. This enhanced precision is achieved through the elimination of unphysical artifacts, specifically the spurious peak often observed in transfer-matrix calculations caused by approximating sharp interface profiles with smooth ones in the complex-sinematic representation. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the analytical prediction of resonance peak positions in various one-dimensional periodic systems, including those featuring sharp interfaces and abrupt changes in the profile.

In the field of information retrieval, the challenge of Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNERT) involves identifying relevant entities within unstructured free text that pertain to a user's query. Previous studies have primarily focused on utilizing supervised learning to train models that predict entity relevance based on the probability of a user clicking on it. However, these models often fail to leverage the abundant unsupervised feedback generated by actual user interactions. This paper introduces a novel approach to leverage this unsupervised feedback by redefining the CNERT task as a semi-supervised learning problem. Our method employs a "dual-contrastive" framework that leverages both positive and negative examples to refine model performance. Specifically, a local contrastive loss function operates on hard negative samples to enhance sample discrimination, while a complementary strategy applies regularization to a local classifier. This regularization forces the classifier to align its outputs with those of a global classifier, ensuring the overall system learns a more robust and accurate relevance assessment. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art methods on the widely-used TREC-CBERT dataset.

Temporal visualizations are frequently integrated with other data views, such as network graphs or geospatial maps, to support interactive exploration. In these scenarios, a temporal plot typically illustrates the evolution of a specific subset of nodes or edges over time, while the accompanying display offers broader context. We introduce a new technique that renders time-varying temporal plots capable of rendering time-varying temporal visualizations. We call this approach "Time Travel," which allows users to navigate through time by clicking on different points along a timeline, effectively revealing hidden patterns and relationships within complex datasets. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate how Time Travel can be effectively applied to various domains, including social networks, biological systems, and financial markets.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant potential in modeling relational data, a capability particularly vital for Electronic Health Records (EHRs) given their capacity to represent diverse entity types and connections. Nevertheless, EHRs present unique challenges due to their inherent heterogeneity and scarcity, which complicate the application of standard GNNs. To address these issues, this study introduces a heterogenous graph learning framework that integrates a multi-view learning approach with graph-based regularization. By constructing a heterogenous graph from EHRs and applying view-specific feed-forward layers alongside multi-view regularization, the model effectively captures both intra-view and inter-view relationships. Experimental results indicate that this architecture surpasses existing methods in accuracy, offering a robust solution for EHR analysis.

This study investigates the influence of ionic size on how electrolytes behave near confined, flexible charged surfaces. We developed an analytical framework to calculate the effective surface charge and electric field, finding that larger ions result in a reduced effective charge and field strength. This outcome stems from the screening effect of counterions accumulating in the low-potential zone adjacent to the surface. Our theoretical predictions align with molecular dynamics simulations, which demonstrate that this concentration of counterions induces an electrostatic repulsion between polymer segments, leading to the expansion of the soft interface.

Software requirements are essential for defining the functional and non-functional constraints of a system, yet their volume and complexity often make manual extraction difficult. This study investigates the application of state-of-the-art BERT models to automatically derive these requirements from software design documents. Our analysis evaluates BERT's performance against alternative approaches, including fastText and ELMo, and examines the impact of pre-training on model efficacy. The results demonstrate that BERT not only surpasses the competing models but also delivers strong performance in this natural language processing task.

This study addresses the challenge of minimizing average user energy consumption in multi-user, multi-relay systems by optimizing relay selection and power allocation. Specifically, it investigates a scenario where a single source communicates with $K$ users via $L$ potential relays. To tackle this NP-hard optimization problem, we introduce a low-complexity, closed-form solution based on a one-dimensional search. Furthermore, we derive an efficient closed-form algorithm for a specific subclass of this problem. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve near-optimal performance with significantly reduced computational complexity.

We investigate the spin-orbit (SO) coupling effects on many-body bound states within a two-dimensional topological insulator, specifically a HgTe quantum well, in the presence of magnetic impurities. Our findings indicate that SO interactions shift the peaks of the local spectral function associated with the Yu-Shrabin-Rydberg (YSR) effect. Furthermore, we observe a pronounced enhancement in the amplitude of these YSR resonances when magnetic atoms or dimers are arranged in concentric circles. By analyzing these characteristics, we propose a strategy for manipulating spin-polarized Yusr states using a potential spintronic application.

The NA62 collaboration at the CERN SpS has conducted a search for the rare decay process K+ → π+ ν̄ν. The study utilized 1.8 fb⁻¹ of data from an incident beam of 4 GeV kinetic-energy protons, employing a kaon sample generated via the K+ → μ+ ν(μ) decay channel. The event selection strategy imposed stringent cuts on missing energy and missing transverse momentum to identify potential K+ → π+ ν̄ signals. The observed event count in the signal region was consistent with the background expectation of 0.02 ± 0.02 events derived from sideband analysis. Consequently, the experiment established a branching fraction limit of Br(K+ → π+ ν̄) < 6.8 × 10⁻⁹ at a 90% confidence level, representing the most stringent constraint to date. This result aligns with the Standard Model prediction of Br(K+ → π+ ν̄) = (2.48 ± 0.01) × 10⁻⁸.

We introduce a novel framework designed to register LiDAR scans in environments cluttered with both static and dynamic objects. Standard registration techniques relying on feature matching often fail when point-to-point or edge-to-edge correlations are disrupted by dynamic changes. To address this, we propose a new approach that links line segments from two separate scans to a pre-trained global model, thereby filtering out local noise. This strategy relies on the premise that in dynamic settings, a significant portion of scene geometry remains static across time steps. We further present a method to automatically identify these stable regions to enhance registration accuracy. Experiments conducted on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Deep learning approaches are widely used in remote sensing, yet they typically demand vast quantities of labeled data that are often difficult and costly to obtain. This study introduces a novel method for semantic segmentation of satellite imagery that leverages unlabeled data, utilizing a self-supervised framework to train a backbone network. This network subsequently transfers its knowledge to a decoder, which is refined using only a small amount of available labeled data. Experiments conducted on the SEN1-2 dataset demonstrate that the proposed architecture surpasses existing state-of-the-art models in performance.

Time-resolved electron diffraction reveals that in metallic nickel, the non-linear absorption increase at high pulse fluences is driven by the non-uniform redistribution of electrons. Specifically, electrons are driven from the outer edge of the Brillouin zone into the center, altering the absorption characteristics. This electron distribution shift occurs simultaneously with the initiation of lattice heating, which subsequently triggers a phase transition to a non-crystalline state.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where subtle, undetectable alterations to inputs cause incorrect classifications. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) offer a promising solution by creating synthetic training data to enhance robustness. This study presents a new approach leveraging GANs to synthesize adversarial samples for augmenting training datasets, thereby improving attack detection. Experimental results indicate that this method effectively increases DNN robustness against adversarial attacks.

Multi-center data is essential for developing robust machine learning models for MS lesion segmentation, yet privacy regulations often prevent the creation of unified, large-scale datasets. To address this, we introduce a strategy for segmenting MS lesions by training on separate datasets from different hospitals using experience replay. This approach enables the exchange of experience across institutions without transferring raw patient data, thereby adhering to strict data protection standards. Our proposed method involves two distinct experience replay mechanisms: one for exchanging segmentations and another for exchanging activation maps. We evaluated this framework on the MultiSite MS lesion segmentation challenge, comparing it against baseline methods and other group submissions. Our results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the baseline and ranks among the top solutions in the competition.

We demonstrate that a novel type of metric comparison, introduced by the authors in previous work [arXiv:1905.00569], is capable of establishing continuity for optimal transport. This approach is applied to derive the optimal transport-based continuity of the optimal transport-based the Brakke flow, as well as other related applications.

Hybrid models that blend domain expertise with data-driven approaches have gained traction, offering the potential to enhance data efficiency and model interpretability. However, their performance hinges on the accuracy of the domain rules employed. Since these rules are often imperfect in practical applications, there is a critical need to assess how effectively such hybrid models can handle flawed inputs. This study addresses this gap by examining data efficiency within regression tasks using a comprehensive benchmark of both perfect and imperfect domain knowledge. The results indicate that while hybrid models excel when their knowledge is accurate, they underperform compared to purely data-driven basings when that knowledge contains errors. Furthermore, a proposed uncertainty quantification method successfully identifies cases where incorporating domain knowledge is beneficial, even in scenarios involving noisy or flawed inputs.

The mass accumulation of molecular cores is hypothesized to fuel massive star formation. However, the extent to which cores directly convert their mass into stars remains uncertain, as cores are dynamic entities that evolve over time. We introduce a novel methodology to determine the mass-to-star formation rate (M/SFR) of cores by analyzing the statistical distribution of their excitation temperatures. Our findings indicate that this ratio is not a fixed constant but varies depending on core size and environmental context. Specifically, larger cores generally exhibit higher M/SFR values, whereas cores situated in denser regions tend to have lower M/SFR values. These observations align with the concept that massive stars emerge through a multi-stage process, where cores progressively expand and subsequently undergo contraction.

The detection of gravitational waves from mergers between stellar-mass black holes has prompted speculation regarding Population III primordial black holes (PBHs) as a potential source for black holes in the $10-100 M_\odot$ range. This study investigates whether PBH microlensing signals could provide independent confirmation of such a Population III origin. We analyze the OGLE-III microlensing dataset, which has been identified as a potential source for detecting evolved stellar black hole remnants via microlensing. Our findings indicate that the OGLE-III sample contains approximately 100 events attributed to PBHs, a number that vastly exceeds those from the OGLE-II survey. Specifically, we anticipate roughly 100 PBH microlensing events, compared to only about 10 events from black holes formed from stellar evolution, assuming a mean PBH mass of $30 M_\odot$.

We investigate the equilibrium states of a two-dimensional system comprising active Brownian particles confined within a circular domain and subject to an external potential. Our analysis focuses on the effects of both particle activity and confinement, particularly examining how activity induces a phase transition from a radially ordered crystal to a frustrated polar crystal. This transition occurs at a specific activity threshold, where the free energy difference between these phases becomes negligible. At a packing density exceeding 0.5, a distinct shift arises from a radially ordered crystal to a frustrated polar crystal, characterized by the emergence of a finite polar order parameter and a non-zero radial density profile. Furthermore, we observe that the radial density profile exhibits oscillations, with their amplitude increasing as activity levels rise.

Pretrained language models have become essential components in numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks. While the success of these models is often attributed to their massive-scale pretraining, language models frequently incorporate special tokens that can obscure critical information. This study investigates how various kinds of special tokens influence downstream task performance. We demonstrate that diverse types of these tokens exert different effects on downstream performance. We also show that while models with special tokens achieve superior results on downstream tasks compared to those without, this superior performance does not always translate to better loss scores. We propose a masking strategy to mitigate the negative impact of special tokens during the final pretraining stage, showing that it significantly improves results on multiple benchmarks. Additionally, we present a new type of token designed to boost performance on core NLP benchmarks, including question answering, natural language inference, and machine reading comprehension.

We propose two distinct frameworks: one grounded in the concept of a classifier and the other in that of a function approximator. To assess which approach is superior, we introduce a decision metric and formulate the problem as an optimization task. We then develop two neural architectures to address these frameworks, training them on a set of examples derived from mathematical laws. The study investigates the dynamic heterogeneity within a binary glass-former, utilizing a coarse-grained model that incorporates a two-body potential derived from a radial distribution function alongside a four-body effective potential capable of reproducing the distinct temporal decay of correlation functions. We demonstrate that this effective potential, which varies with time, can describe the slow relaxation characteristic of glass-forming liquids by accounting for spatially fluctuating interaction strengths. Furthermore, we find that the variance in these effective potentials serves as a marker for dynamic heterogeneity and aligns with the extent of correlation observed in intermediate scattering functions. Additionally, we establish that the magnitude of dynamic heterogeneity is intrinsically tied to the system's dynamics through two separate thermodynamic scaling relationships.

Natural Language Inference (NLI) has become a primary benchmark for assessing the capabilities of transformer models. While these models have achieved remarkable human-level accuracy on most NLI tasks, they frequently falter when encountering negation. This study investigates how various categories of negation impact NLI performance within transformer architectures. Our findings reveal that (i) different negation types exhibit varying impacts on models, with some causing more significant disruptions than others, and (ii) models generally perform better on positive premises compared to those containing negative statements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating more diverse positive data substantially improves model performance on previously challenging instances of negation within NLI tasks.

Sequential models, particularly recurrent neural networks, are widely used for neural machine translation. However, their fixed hidden states limit their ability to capture long-term dependencies, hindering the generation of accurate translations. To address this, we introduce a look-ahead (LA) mechanism that incorporates future context into the decoder's state. By integrating this into the transformer architecture, our proposed Transformer-LA model achieved an average improvement of 0.7 BLEU score on three datasets compared to the standard Transformer baseline. Furthermore, the model demonstrated enhanced robustness, reducing the degradation in translation quality when vocabulary size is reduced.

We present a novel formula for the symplectic Novikov ring of a tangent bundle's sphere bundle, expressed through the curvature weights of a toric action on a Kähler bundle. This approach builds upon earlier work by Lott and Foulis, adapting their methodology to cases where the torus acts on the cotangent bundle of a manifold.

We examine thermal entropy and thermal two-point functions of the stress-energy tensor for three-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) constructed via deformation of superconformal theories. Our findings indicate that thermal entropy decreases monotonically as the coupling strengthens and that the stress-energy tensor two-point functions exhibit a dependence on temperature and coupling that aligns with established universality constraints.

This paper extends the methodology of double Laplace transforms, previously applied to pricing standard Asian options by Laughton and Sentana (1990), to cover options with non-maturing payoff structures. Furthermore, it demonstrates that utilizing the one-sided Laplace transform significantly accelerates the computational efficiency required to price these options.

The nature of the diffuse gamma-ray background (DGR) remains a longstanding issue in high-energy astrophysics. This study investigates the DGR's origin using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (Fermi-LAT), which recorded 1.5 million gamma-ray events from 1,000 galaxy clusters. Our analysis reveals that the gamma-ray flux from these clusters correlates with their X-ray luminosity, a relationship consistent with emission driven by hadronic proton-proton collisions. Furthermore, we find that the observed flux from these clusters is insufficient to account for the DGR, indicating that galaxy clusters alone cannot explain this background. Consequently, we conclude that the DGR likely originates from sources other than galaxy clusters.

We investigate a class of inflation models characterized by sharp features in the background evolution, which generate distinct imprints in the primordial curvature perturbation's power spectrum and induce significant features in primordial non-Gaussianities (NGs). Focusing on a specific model where a sharp feature appears within a single interaction term, we demonstrate that this approach can yield diverse observational signatures. By tuning the parameters, the model can reproduce the signatures of previously studied mechanisms, including resonant NGs, enhanced single-field NGs, and NGs arising from feature-induced bispectrum modulations. Furthermore, this framework is applicable to scenarios involving multiple sharp features. Consequently, this model offers a versatile theoretical tool for investigating how different inflationary mechanisms produce observable effects in NGs.

Creating human-understandable descriptions for the internal representations of deep visual networks is a crucial yet difficult challenge. This paper introduces LaViSE, a novel approach that generates descriptive sentences about convolutional neural network (CNN) features by leveraging the CLEVR synthetic dataset. LaViSE employs a two-stage pipeline: first, a visual language model pre-trained on Microsoft COCO is fine-tuned on CLEVR data to create a joint scene representation embedding; second, this embedding is decoded into natural language sentences describing feature characteristics. To address the limitations of CLEVR's fixed vocabulary, LaViSE dynamically constructs descriptions using attributes and objects detected within COCV during its fine-tuning phase. Evaluation on CLEVR demonstrates that LaViSE produces more accurate and logically consistent descriptions compared to prior methods, underscoring the value of heterogeneous datasets for visual description tasks. Furthermore, qualitative analysis of descriptions for real-world datasets like ImageNet and CIFAR-10 reveals that LaViSE successfully captures meaningful patterns in convoluted features.

This study examines the electronic and optical properties of Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{10}$, a two-dimensional cuprate superconductor, using density functional theory. The findings reveal that this material shares a structural similarity with one-dimensional counterparts, suggesting that high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates may stem from anisotropic three-dimensional characteristics.

This research investigates how travel time to HIV treatment centers influences patient engagement, specifically examining whether the impact varies based on individuals' familiarity with their commute duration. Utilizing data from the *SEARCH* (Study of HIV Care Retention in Africa) longitudinal study, we apply a dynamic discrete choice model to estimate how changes in travel time affect retention likelihood, accounting for unobserved heterogeneity. Our findings indicate that travel time significantly reduces treatment retention, yet this negative effect is mitigated for individuals who are already familiar with their commute duration.

This study examines the magnetic phase transitions in MnSi, a prototypical chiral magnet, utilizing a microscopic model that incorporates both nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor exchange interactions. Our analysis reveals that a negative magnetic field induces a shift from a metastable skyrmion lattice to a non-uniform phase, which eventually stabilizes into a conical structure at high field strengths. Furthermore, we calculate the magnetic field dependence of the helical winding number and skyrmion lattice density.

This study introduces the concept of singular ARMA models to expand the framework of High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models. We establish the partial ergodic theorem for singular ARMA processes and examine their properties within the context of dynamic factor models. Additionally, we propose a partial maximum likelihood estimation method capable of handling both singular and non-singular scenarios, with performance validated through numerical simulations.

We examine the iterative resolution of the sum of two involutive mappings $T$ and $U$ defined on a Hilbert space. By leveraging the fixed points of the Meyer proximal mapping, we establish, assuming the range of $T$ is the entire Hilbert space, that these points coincide with the solutions of a specific equilibrium problem. Building upon this foundation, we introduce a novel iterative algorithm designed to approximate common fixed points of $T$ and $U$. We demonstrate the method's strong convergence to such common fixed points when the composition $T \circ U$ is a strictly pseudocontractive operator. Furthermore, we extend these findings to include a finite collection of strictly pseudocontractive operators.

A primary challenge in deep learning is establishing the reliability of predictive models, which is often difficult to quantify using traditional methods. We introduce a Bayesian framework that treats the predictive distribution of a neural network as a prior distribution for Bayesian inference. By employing a small ensemble of Bayesian neural networks as priors, we calculate a posterior distribution for the initial approach. Subsequently, a more efficient strategy utilizes a single wide Bayesian neural network with multiple outputs to represent the entire posterior distribution. This streamlined method offers a computationally efficient and effective means of establishing uncertainty for both regression and classification tasks.

This study introduces a novel, fully implicit, finite-volume method designed to simulate dynamos within the solar and stellar regimes. This approach captures the generation of magnetic fields by turbulent motions and their subsequent transport by mean flows. By utilizing a fully implicit scheme, the method effectively captures the extremely long timescales inherent to dynamos, which are usually too lengthy for standard explicit numerical techniques. A primary innovation is the construction of a unified Jacobian matrix that encapsulates the complete system of governing equations, thereby enabling stable convergence even with super-critical magnetic magnetic Reynolds numbers. This capability allows for the simulation of dynamos where turbulent impacts dominate mean flow dynamics. Numerical tests on a simplified spherical geometry, featuring both mean flows and turbulence aligned with the equatorial plane, demonstrate the method's efficacy. Results indicate that while dynamos can generate magnetic fields in this configuration, the resulting structures remain largely constrained to latitudinal bands due to the suppression of axial magnetic field components by turbulence.

We have conducted a comprehensive investigation of the outflows in the molecular outflows of the molecular galaxy NGC 4945, a system renowned for its strong outflows. Utilizing high-resolution data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we identified a compact, blueshifted outflow originating from the galaxy's nucleus. This outflow is characterized by a total mass outflow rate of $\sim 1.5$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ and a terminal velocity of $\sim 200$ km s$^{-1}$. Additionally, we detected a spatially extended molecular outflow extending $\sim 1$ kpc from the nucleus, with a mass outflow rate of $\sim 0.5$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$ and a terminal velocity of $\sim 250$ km s$^{-1}$. Our findings indicate that the outflow is highly collimated along the galaxy's minor axis, a behavior attributed to the combined effects of a bar and a spiral arm. The study further reveals that the outflow is driven by a central starburst, a conclusion supported by the correlation between the outflow's properties and the starburst's energy output. The results also suggest that the outflow is a significant contributor to the galaxy's chemical evolution, potentially playing a role in the regulation of star formation.

We propose a class of nonstationary generalized linear mixed (SGLMs) designed for integration over nonuniform grids, which we demonstrate are equivalent to implicit-explicit linear multistep methods. This study investigates their convergence properties, establishing that they achieve second-order accuracy under reasonable conditions. Furthermore, we show how to construct an optimal preconditioner for the normal equations of our scheme, ensuring that the condition number of the resulting system matrix remains bounded as the step size approaches zero. We also present numerical experiments that validate our theoretical findings and compare the performance of our scheme against existing methods.

We demonstrate that under specific conditions, a unique solution exists. Additionally, we establish the presence of a unique positive definite solution for this equation.

MuMuPy is an open-source Python tool designed to calculate transition probabilities for dimuonium and other bound states composed of heavy bosons. It determines transition rates for all spin-conserving and spin-flipping processes involving one- and two-photon exchanges. Users can further extend the code to incorporate additional interaction types, such as Z boson exchanges or multi-photon transitions.

We introduce a novel utility function designed to optimize investment portfolios by simultaneously accounting for both absolute and relative wealth levels. The study examines optimization challenges under this framework for both one-period and multi-period models, providing solutions for specific cases involving log-utility. The proposed approach is applied to rebalancing strategies, generating optimal policies through a backtesting analysis. Results indicate that when wealth is high, a constant rebalancing strategy performs best; conversely, when wealth is low, optimal policies suggest rebalancing at shorter intervals.

We report on a spectroscopic study of 10 Local Green Pea galaxies using the 3.6-meter Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope, analyzing their emission-line properties via the 3D-COS instrument. These results are compared with data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) on 10 early Universe analogues (Green Peas) identified in the COSMOS field. The analysis reveals that the local Green Peas exhibit higher ionization parameters, lower metal abundances, and lower ionization rates compared to their early Universe counterparts. Additionally, the local sample shows lower dust-to-gas ratios and lower star formation rates. These findings suggest that the properties of these early Universe analogues resemble those of young galaxies in the local cosmos.

This model serves as a foundational representation for the interaction between conduction electrons and their surrounding bosonic environments, exemplified by electron-phonon coupling and electron-electron interactions.
