We demonstrate that the linear word problem holds for the quotient of the braided Thompson's groups by their inner automorphisms, implying that these groups have a linear divergence and a linear isoperimetric constant.

This work outlines our approach to fine-tuning a Retrieval Augment Generation (RAG) system, which inherently involves addressing two distinct challenges: optimizing a dual-objective loss function for a dual-tower retrieval architecture and generating responses conditioned on a specific graph structure. Our solution to the first issue employs a weighted average of standard dual-tower losses, where weights are determined by the relative performance of each tower. To resolve the second challenge, we represent answer spans as graph nodes and model the answer generation process as a path prediction task within a pointer network framework. Experiments conducted on the Natural Questions dataset demonstrate that our proposed Fine-Tuned RAG (FT-RAG) method achieves superior performance compared to a baseline model that relies solely on the generator's pre-trained knowledge.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior as $n \to \infty$ of orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle under weights $w^{(n)}(\mathrm{d}\theta) = e^{n\cos\theta}\,\mathrm{d}\theta$. For these weights, we derive explicit formulas for monic polynomials and the corresponding polynomials of the second kind. Additionally, we investigate the associated $n\times n$ Toeplitz matrices and the corresponding $n\times n$ minors. By utilizing techniques from asymptotic analysis, these results are derived through the application of a Riemann-Hilbert approach.

Annotation workloads for complex tasks, such as automatic summarization, are often prohibitively expensive and time-consuming to source from qualified human workers. We propose an innovative qualification pipeline designed to secure high-quality labels by directly targeting qualified candidates, bypassing the need for preliminary screening through a two-tiered approach. First, we deploy a quick, automated first-tier system to filter out low-performing crowdworkers. Subsequently, those who pass this initial hurdle are recruited for the main, more rigorous labeling task. We evaluated this pipeline's efficacy on a dataset built for an automatic summarization task and found that it effectively filters out poor performers while maintaining label quality comparable to that achieved by fully screened annotators.

Spatial-temporal two-stream networks are widely recognized for generating effective 2D representations in video for text-video retrieval tasks. However, these methods often overlook the intricate interplay between a video's inherent content and a query's semantic requirements. To address this, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel approach that leverages two-stream representations to learn a joint, high-quality joint representation tailored for specific retrieval tasks. TS2-Net employs two parallel branches: a two-stream branch that captures detailed spatiotemporal features, and a two-stream feature fusion branch that learns a joint representation by integrating the two-stream features. In our experiments, we demonstrate that TS2-Net significantly improves the quality of spatiotemporal representations for text-video retrieval tasks. Furthermore, we show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a large margin on multiple benchmark datasets.

At the LHC, rare top decays and the specific $\bar{t}tH$ scenario offer valuable probes for new physics. We demonstrate that, within composite Higgs frameworks, these rare decays and $\bar{t}tH$ production provide complementary constraints on the model's parameter space. We also show that, for a Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV, the combination of LHC data and future electron-positron collider results can tightly restrict composite model parameters, potentially confirming new physics even if it manifests solely through the $\bar{t}tH$ channel.

Hybrid random networks are constructed by superimposing a preferential attachment tree onto a regular network structure. This study examines their statistical properties, including degree distributions, clustering coefficients, and path lengths. We demonstrate that both in- and out-degree distributions within hybrid random networks align with those of standalone preferential attachment networks. Additionally, the clustering coefficients are governed by the underlying regular network, whereas the path lengths result from the combined characteristics of both components.

This study introduces a novel interference classification approach for underwater acoustic networks, grounded in the analysis of signal characteristics and the implementation of a deep learning framework. The methodology employs a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the cross-entropy and kurtosis of signals, followed by a fully connected neural network (FNN) to synthesize these outputs for determining signal categories. The framework was evaluated across two distinct scenarios: interference from the same technology and cross-technology interference. The results indicate that the average classification accuracy reaches 98.4% in the same-technology scenario and 94.1% in the cross-technology scenario. Furthermore, the accuracy in the cross-technology scenario improves with an increased number of mixed signal samples.

We demonstrate that the influence of a specific spacetime structure, known as the "Khan" metric, on scalar particles described by the Klein-Gordon equation gives rise to novel phenomena absent in standard flat-space scenarios. Notably, this interaction generates an effective spatial topology resembling a cylinder, which in turn produces distinctive interference patterns. Furthermore, gravity induces a non-trivial Aharonov-Bohm-type phase shift. These findings are derived through an analysis of the Klein-Gordon equation, which serves as the relativistic quantum analog to the Klein-Gordon Hamiltonian, highlighting how external fields can fundamentally alter quantum particle behavior.

The twist-two, orbital-angular-momentum-dependent generalized parton distribution $E$ is notoriously difficult to measure, particularly within fixed-target frameworks, due to the experimental constraints required to access its specific kinematic variables. This study investigates the potential for extracting $E$ in ultra-peripheral heavy-ion collisions by analyzing a hadron produced alongside a virtual photon that interacts with a second hadron. We demonstrate that azimuthal asymmetries in both the differential cross-section for this exclusive process and the longitudinal structure function $F_2^{\text{LFV}}$ arise from non-zero values of $E$. Furthermore, we quantify the necessary luminosity needed to achieve a 10% measurement precision of $E$ in both proton-proton and proton-lead collisions at the LHC, utilizing a proposed future exclusive hadronic tagging apparatus.

The ability to learn linear concepts is considered a fundamental milestone in AI development. Although previous research has explored the link between linear classifiers and the difficulty of rectifying mistakes in high-dimensional settings, this study advances the field by (i) establishing linear classifiers as a robust benchmark for identifying target errors amenable to correction, and (ii) demonstrating their utility in uncovering the root causes of such errors. We evaluate our methodology using a rigorous set of tasks designed to assess various aspects of neural network training and the subsequent debugging of AI models.

We investigate a multi-component Bose–Hubbard model featuring spin-orbit coupling applied exclusively to one of the coupled Bose gases. By examining the system in one dimension with on-site repulsive multi-species interactions, we observe that varying the spin-orbit coupling strength and interaction parameters yields distinct phases, including uniform superfluids, Mott insulators, and phase-separated superfluids. Notably, in the regime of weak spin-orbit coupling and moderate repulsive interactions, the system stabilizes into two specific uniform superfluid states: one where all spin-orbit-coupled atoms occupy a single spin state (polar), and another where the atoms distribute across multiple spin states (bipolar or multicomponent). These unique phases are absent in systems where all atoms possess an internal structure. Furthermore, we analyze the characteristics of the bipolar and multipolar uniform superfluid states, demonstrating that they remain stable against phase separation across a broader range of parameters when compared to the polar configuration.

We establish a framework for finite abelian $p$-groups via sets of saturated chains of Young diagrams, where every such group corresponds to multiple, specific representations. Although these representations appear distinct at first glance, we demonstrate that they are equivalent through the action of a Hecke monoid. Additionally, we examine the categorical structure under this action and explore connections to the representation theory of Hecke algebras associated with finite groups of Lie type.

We explore defects within AdS/CFT frameworks, specifically focusing on how surface and line defects correspond to line and surface probes within dual gravity theories. In the AdS/CFT setting, line defects are treated as fundamental components of the conformal field variable, whereas surface defects function as external sources. Within the dual gravity dual, these translate to a geodesic probe for line defects and a minimal surface probe for those of higher dimensionality, both embedded in anti-de Sitter space. We demonstrate that the finite contributions arising from such surface and line probes are mutually dual, provided the gravitational coupling is appropriately scaled.

Kernel methods are highly effective tools in machine learning, particularly for addressing non-linear challenges. This study introduces a novel model that employs a compact tree structure to represent kernel functions, facilitating the explicit modeling of data properties like homophily and structural anti-homophily. This approach enables the creation of a scalable algorithm capable of solving large-scale machine learning problems efficiently. Extensive experiments across various real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

In-flight production of muons and their subsequent decays are unavoidable characteristics of a muon collider. The resulting neutrinos generate a neutrino fog that can degrade detector performance. This study examines how to mitigate this neutrino fog in detectors for muon colliders by exploring various design strategies. Specifically, we analyze configurations involving a toroidal layout, a tilted beam pipe, and an inclined entrance window. Furthermore, we examine how these design choices influence the angular resolution of the calorimeter and the overall energy measurement precision.

We investigate the impact of Pauli blocking on the excitation spectrum of a three-dimensional bosonic gas in the quantum crossover regime, utilizing a variational approach to study the coupled system of fermions and bosons. The findings indicate that Pauli blocking significantly alters the bosonic excitation spectrum, causing it to deviate from the standard linear behavior and aligning the results with the expected consequences of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Furthermore, the energy of the ground state and the chemical potential of the bosons are computed, with a demonstration that the total ground state energy of the mixed fermion-boson system is lower than that of the bosons alone. This confirms the stability of the system and validates the formation of the polaron.

Although test smells are prevalent in real-world code, the specific impact of these issues on a project's maintainability remains unclear. This study aims to bridge that knowledge gap by examining how software developers perceive the seriousness of test smells and their potential effect on long-term maintainability. To achieve this, the research employs a mixed-methods approach, beginning with a survey of 100 developers to gauge their opinions on smell severity and, subsequently, a follow-up study with 20 developers using a scenario-based questionnaire to explore the consequences of encountering such smells in actual test cases. The findings reveal that developers generally recognize the high severity of test smells and their capacity to undermine maintainability. The scenario analysis further highlights that these issues can lead to significant consequences, including extended maintenance time, a decline in software quality, and heightened bug rates. Ultimately, the results suggest that addressing test smells is crucial for sustaining high-quality testing practices.

This study establishes both the existence of solutions and their uniqueness for a class of integro-differential sweeping processes, contingent upon the kernel's continuity regarding initial values. Furthermore, it derives a Hoffman-type error bound associated with these processes.

We introduce an updated Monte Carlo algorithm for the generation of multi-particle final states within electron-positron collisions, developed under the KKMC framework. This version significantly enhances the probability of including leptons and quark production events compared to the original KKMC. The new approach is integrated into the HERWIG program, which already employs a similar algorithm for similar final states. We have applied this updated algorithm to calculate the cross-sections for electron-positron collisions at the LEP center-of-mass energy level. Additionally, we provide a comparison of the results against the existing KKMC predictions and the predictions from the PYTHIA program.

This study introduces a deep-learning approach to extract inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from noisy electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. The method involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify windows of ECG data as either "beat" or "non-beat." Subsequently, beat-to-beat intervals are derived from the CNN's predictions. We evaluated this model using the noisy version of the publicly available PTB-XL dataset. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art IBI estimation techniques in terms of accuracy.

Truncated Singular Value Decomposition (t-SVD) is a powerful tool for analyzing tensor subspaces, finding extensive use in fields like image processing and data mining. While recent research has introduced a randomized algorithm for computing the t-SVD, it maintains the limitation of requiring multiple passes over the input data tensor. This paper presents a refined randomized algorithm that achieves the same theoretical guarantees as the current state-of-the-art but completes the computation in only a single pass. This method is implemented alongside a highly optimized CUDA version for GPUs, which demonstrates significant speed improvements on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, we apply this algorithm to perform tensor rank minimization, a technique for recovering low-rank tensors from partial observations. Our CUDA-driven approach outperforms the existing fastest CPU-based algorithms by a substantial margin.

Graph Embedding is a foundational technique for graph mining, which maps graph nodes to a lower-dimensional space to facilitate downstream tasks. While extensive research has focused on embedding static graphs, dynamic graphs—characterized by nodes and edges that evolve over time—pose distinct challenges due to their temporal nature. This paper introduces a novel approach to embedding dynamic graphs by leveraging the time-series characteristics of historical data to predict future temporal graphs. Specifically, we propose a self-attention-based architecture to capture dependencies between time-series data points, enabling the anticipation of future structures. Consequently, this predictive capability allows for the extension of static graph embedding methods to handle temporal dynamics. Experimental results on real-world datasets validate the efficacy of this approach, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods.

The $^7$H nucleus has been extensively studied to understand its potential as a candidate for unbound halo nuclear structure. Previous investigations into its two-neutron separation energy and existence as a bound or resonant state yielded conflicting results. This study addresses these discrepancies by examining the $^7$Li($^3$He, t)$^7$Li and $^7$Li($^3$He, $^6$He)$^8$Li reactions at 15 MeV using a radioactive beam. The data were analyzed with the distorted wave impulse approximation to extract the cross-section for the direct $^3$He stripping process, which populates the $^7$H nucleus. The findings indicate that the resonance observed in prior experiments cannot exist as a narrow low-energy state. Furthermore, the study rules out the possibility of $^7$H existing as a bound nucleus or a stable state with a width exceeding 0.1 MeV.

This paper examines solutions to Nirenberg-type problems on half-spheres in $\mathbb{S}^n$ that exhibit a unique degenerate blow-up profile at the boundary point. In contrast to the well-established behavior on full spheres, where solutions display precise asymptotic limits under similar conditions, our analysis reveals that such problems on spherical caps lack similar stable degenerate profiles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these boundary blow-up phenomena are fundamentally linked to the presence of degenerate critical manifolds.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning (SSL) have demonstrated significant efficacy in learning robust embedding spaces, yet they often overlook class-specific discriminative information. This absence of local structure hinders SSL techniques from effectively transferring to downstream tasks like visual recognition. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel Deep Class-wise Discrepancy Loss (DCDL) that enhances existing SSL frameworks by focusing on class-level discriminative details. Our approach operates through two key mechanisms: first, it generates class-wise positive pairs by aggregating augmented samples from the same category, and subsequently, it minimizes the divergence between these constructed pairs and their respective class negatives. This strategy effectively strengthens local structure within the embedding space, thereby improving task transferability. Empirical evaluations across multiple datasets and tasks indicate that our method achieves a substantial performance boost of 2.6% over existing SSL baselines. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengzhengzheng/DCDL.

In the United Kingdom, local tracing partnerships were established to support Test and Trace, the national initiative for identifying and isolating individuals with COVID-19. These partnerships comprised various stakeholders, including local authorities, clinical commissioning groups, and NHS trusts. This paper examines the influence of these partnerships on the operational performance of Test and Trace. Using a quasi-experimental design, the study analyzes data from 120 local areas, comparing contact rates before and after the launch of the partnerships. The findings indicate that while local partnerships did not significantly enhance the overall effectiveness of Test and Trace, they substantially increased contact rates within specific areas. This suggests that the success of the programme was unevenly distributed, with some regions achieving higher contact volumes post-implementation. Consequently, the study recommends that future evaluations of public health interventions should account for the variability in outcomes across different local contexts.

We have conducted a comprehensive study of Melotte 72, an open cluster located in the Cygnus region, by analyzing its stellar population, kinematics, and physical characteristics. The observed stellar distribution includes main-sequence stars, giants, and a small number of white dwarfs, with the latter allowing us to estimate the cluster's age at approximately 100 million years, making it the youngest open cluster in the Cygnus region known to date. By comparing the cluster's radial velocities with the Cygnus OB2 association, we determined that M. 72 shares a common kinematic history, suggesting it is a member of the Cygnus complex. Furthermore, the presence of a stellar mass-to-luminosity ratio of roughly 0.7 indicates that Melotte 72 has not undergone significant mass loss.

This study investigates random field excursions (RFEs) of dimension $d \ge 3$ that terminate upon reaching a bounded set, specifically a ball of radius $R$. We demonstrate that the excursions beyond level $u$ of a normalized RFE exhibit a phase transition at the excursion critical radius $R_c(u)$, shifting from a disordered phase where infinite-excess excursions exist to an ordered phase where only those with sub-exponential decay remain. For dimensions $d \ge 3$, we derive both upper and lower bounds for $R_c(u)$ that are of the same asymptotic order as $u \to \infty$. Additionally, we establish a sharp transition in the $L^p$-norms of the RFE at $R_c(u)$, where the norm remains bounded for $p < d/vol$ and diverges for $p > d/vol$. These findings mirror the phase transition observed in the Ising model.

Direct regression has recently emerged as a competitive approach for camera calibration, offering a streamlined process by eliminating the need for complex multi-step recovery procedures. This study evaluates its performance in an indoor setting, specifically a task involving the estimation of intrinsics for a single lenseye toy eye. By leveraging multiple datasets acquired through a robotic arm-mounted eye that observes a checkerboard across various poses, we employ both classical calibration methods and direct regression to solve for the eye's parameters. The results indicate that direct regression consistently outperforms traditional methods, achieving more accurate calibration with lower intrinsic parameters.

In this work, we introduce a reinforcement learning approach that integrates a pre-trained, structure-abiding policy to derive learned constraints for solving a specified task. These constraints, which represent a set of forbidden states in a continuous space, are generated by the structure-abiding policy and can subsequently be utilized to define task-specific regions, such as obstacle areas in navigation problems. Our numerical results demonstrate that this method yields robust and generalizable constraints that effectively facilitate planning.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission is a space-based astrometry observatory designed to map the Milky Way with unprecedented precision. GAIA achieves this by measuring the positions, motions, and basic properties of over a billion stars, delivering a three-dimensional view of our Galaxy. The mission's data pipeline processes raw observations into calibrated catalogues through a multi-stage process, with the final phase applying complex Galactic models to refine astrometric results. This study introduces the methodology behind that final step, detailing the specific models applied to various catalogues for the first and second data releases.

We present a unified framework for addressing standard graph challenges, particularly Vertex Cover and MaxCut, leveraging an algorithmic approach based on an approximation scheme derived from tree decomposition. Our method's efficiency is directly tied to the quality of the given tree decomposition; specifically, an input with $O(\log n)$ height and approximation ratio of $O(\log^* n)$ yields results in linear time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this framework can be adapted to solve a broader range of classical problems, including Dominating Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and Minimum $s$-$t$ Cut.

The continuous clustering coefficient proposed by Zhang and Horváth has been widely adopted in network science literature. This study examines its behavior and interpretation by comparing it against a new continuous metric, $C_{new}$, which is also grounded in local node neighborhoods. We evaluate both measures across random graphs, random geometric graphs, and empirical networks. Our findings indicate that $C_{new}$ outperforms the Zhang–Horvát coefficient in numerous scenarios. Specifically, $C_{new}$ maintains robust behavior and a consistent meaning regardless of mean degree, average clustering levels, network type, or whether nodes are constrained to geometric locations. In contrast, the Zhang–Horváth metric can become unstable under certain conditions and even yield negative values. Additionally, $C_{new}$ demonstrates a stronger correlation with both global clustering coefficients and key structural features like triangle density and three-node subgraph counts. Consequently, $C_{new}$ offers a more reliable measure of local clustering for diverse network types.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently gained significant attention for their ability to forecast complex system behaviors. However, due to their reliance on stochastic optimization, the accuracy of PINNs remains uncertain, particularly when applied to safety-critical scenarios. This paper introduces a framework for certifying the errors of fully connected feedforward neural networks, including PINNPs, by leveraging rigorous a posteriori error estimation. The methodology involves constructing a surrogate model that bounds the discrepancy between a feedforward network's output and the underlying target function. This is achieved by formulating and solving a convex optimization problem, where the objective function represents this approximation error. By applying feedforward analysis to the problem's components, we derive guaranteed error limits for the surrogate model. These bounds subsequently enable the certification of prediction errors for the primary feedforward networks. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through experiments on a simple benchmark case and applications in high-stakes PINNN contexts, such as predicting turbulent fluid flow and assessing the structural integrity of aircraft wings.

This article introduces a new methodology for air pollution modeling that relies on spatial covariance models (SCMs) to represent the complex, high-dimensional relationships between meteorological conditions and air quality. The proposed framework utilizes Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to construct a precise surrogate model capable of approximating existing, data-intensive air pollution models. We demonstrate that this approach offers significant advantages by facilitating rapid scenario assessments, enabling the integration of uncertain inputs, and supporting the creation of data-driven emulators for model order reduction. Furthermore, the study presents the development of a new methodology for constructing these surrogate models using a hierarchical GPR framework that incorporates hierarchical GPR to account for spatial covariance. The method is validated using data from a real-world air pollution dataset, showing that the resulting model achieves high predictive accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency.

Topological superconductors are expected to host Majorana zero modes (MZMs), which could enable non-Abelian braiding and a topological quantum computer. However, similar MZM-like signatures can also emerge from non-Majorana phenomena, such as Andreev bound states (ABS). While thermal effects on ABS are well-understood, their thermal impact on MZMs remains less studied. This study investigates how temperature influences the tunneling density of states (TDoS) for both cases. We find that the sharp zero-energy peak caused by non-Majorana effects broadens into a U-shaped feature as temperature increases, a result confirmed by experimental tunneling data from a topological semiconductor nanowire. In contrast, the MZM peak persists at elevated temperatures, exhibiting only minor changes. Additionally, we demonstrate that AC Josephson currents can effectively distinguish between ABS and MZMs. These findings suggest that studying finite-temperature effects provides a powerful tool for disentangling ABS from true MZMs in experiments.

This study addresses the challenge of model selection and subspace clustering within linear bandit frameworks. We propose a novel algorithm that simultaneously performs model selection and dimension reduction while achieving a regret bound of $\tilde{O}(d^2\sqrt{T})$. This performance matches the current state-of-the-art for the specific case of selecting among an unknown number of subspaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to determine the count of these subspaces and validate our approach through numerical experiments. The spectral conditions underlying our model selection and clustering procedures offer valuable insights for the design of future algorithms.

The Valley Hall effect (VHE) was originally proposed to explain the anomalous Hall effect in systems lacking ferromagnetism. However, a significant ambiguity remains regarding how to interpret the measured conductivity: it could arise from VHE or the orbital Hall effect (OHE). Unlike the VHE, the OHE originates from spin-orbit coupling, which provides a distinct theoretical framework. This review outlines the origins of both VHE and OHE, examines the conditions under which they coexist, and analyzes the factors influencing the measured conductivity. By clarifying the distinctions between these phenomena, this work aims to resolve the longstanding confusion surrounding the interpretation of the anomalous hall conductivity.

This paper introduces a new framework for adversarial machine learning rooted in Reinforcement Learning (RL), leveraging Q-learning to navigate the complex, high-dimensional state spaces typical of this field. By treating adversarial training as a sequential decision process, our approach directly optimizes Q-functions rather than computing gradients through intricate state transitions. This distinct optimization strategy offers a more straightforward pathway for training robust models, circumventing the computational complexities of gradient propagation in complex state spaces. Furthermore, our proposed Q-learning-based framework is designed to be versatile, capable of addressing key challenges such as adversarial classification, evasion of out-of-distribution samples, and model inversion attacks.

We introduce a novel method for matching sources between images that rely on a probabilistic framework for estimating associations. This approach generates probabilistic estimates for individual source pairings, which are subsequently aggregated to produce a posterior probability map representing the overall alignment between source catalogs. The method utilizes photometry to enhance the accuracy of these estimates. Specifically, we employ a Gaussian Mixture Model to derive probability density functions for source brightness values, using these distributions to refine the reliability of individual match estimates. By incorporating photometric data, the system significantly boosts performance, particularly in scenarios involving sparse sources. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this method to identify galaxies in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds within the Gaia-ESO survey, utilizing the photometric catalogs generated by the SkyMapper telescope.

We introduce a new strong partition relation for cards that serves as a generalization of Erd\H{o}s-Rado's classical theorem. Our theorem states: if $\kappa$ is a regular cardinal and $\lambda$ is any cardinal, then there exists a stationary subset $S \subseteq \lambda^+$ such that for all $\alpha \in S$, the condition $\lambda^{\text{cf}(\alpha)} < \text{cf}(\kappa)$ holds. We define such a pair as satisfying the $(\kappa, \lambda)$-nowhere-stationary property. This relation is shown to be equivalent to the statement that the collection of cardinals failing this property for a fixed $\lambda$ forms a stationary subset of $\lambda^+$ in any equivalent formulation.

Our proof technique relies on a stationary version of a combinatorial principle that is well-established in the context of partition calculus. By leveraging this principle, we derive significant corollaries, including a stationary variant of Erd\H{o}s' theorem and a stationary extension of Silver's theorem. Additionally, we explore the connections between our main result and the $\square_\lambda$-principle, providing a stationary generalization of Shelah's theorem that applies when $\square_\lambda$ holds.

Semantic Web technologies enable the distribution of knowledge across networks of interconnected documents, utilizing ontologies to define concepts and their interrelations. While ontology visualization is crucial for understanding this structured information, existing solutions often suffer from limited flexibility, poor scalability, and inadequate support for customization and extension. OntoPlot addresses these limitations by offering a user-friendly, extensible framework that renders ontological structures as force-directed graphs. This tool allows users to tailor visual outputs to specific domains and conceptual models and supports the integration of additional data sources, such as natural language definitions. Furthermore, OntoPlot employs a hierarchical force-directed graph algorithm that improves the clarity of visualizations for large-scale ontologies.

Converting images from one domain to another using CycleGAN has proven effective, yet its application to point clouds remains under-explored. This study introduces the first implementation of CycleGAN for transforming 3D lidar data into 2D camera images. We evaluate the method on the SemanticKITTI dataset, which contains paired lidar-camera data. Results indicate that this approach retains characteristic details from the source domain and produces meaningful outputs. Furthermore, integrating CycleGAN with a pre-trained ResNet architecture enhances object detection performance in the translated images.

The advent of deep generative models has marked a turning point in artificial intelligence, enabling the synthesis of highly realistic sensory data. Recent progress has driven these models toward mastering complex distributions found in actual environments. However, despite this success, there remains a lack of consensus on the degree to which such models truly understand reality. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to assess models by querying them for questions they cannot answer, thereby exposing their limitations. Our approach utilizes a question-answering system grounded in world knowledge to formulate inquiries that demand extensive global context. To demonstrate the efficacy of this framework, we apply it to state-of-the-art text-image synthesis architectures. Our findings reveal that even the most advanced models struggle with questions rooted in general world knowledge, suggesting that their grasp of reality is still incomplete.

This study employs a novel computational framework to examine thermal diffusion in binary molecular gas mixtures subjected to a temperature gradient. Utilizing the framework's ability to handle complex molecular geometries, we modeled rigid and flexible structures, explicitly incorporating intramolecular temperatures and temperatures specific to vibrational and translational degrees of freedom. Results indicate that molecular flexibility significantly impacts the thermal diffusion factor; specifically, thermal diffusion is enhanced in scenarios where intramolecular temperatures are elevated relative to the translational temperature.

However, these approaches typically demand substantial computational resources for both training and inference. This study investigates whether fine-tuning smaller models can match the performance of these larger transformers for AES tasks. We introduce a self-supervised learning approach for converting false-positive suppression challenges into box re-ranking problems, thereby enabling area estimation without annotated data. This transformation leverages the observation that suppressing false positives is equivalent to re-ranking boxes to eliminate those with the least intersection over union (IoU) against ground truths. We derive a self-supervised loss function that aligns with this re-ranking strategy, which can be optimized using standard object detectors. We prove that this method yields a lower bound on the IoU between generated and true segmentations. Empirical results on the challenging COCO benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves an IoU of 0.50, establishing a new state-of-the-art for unsupervised area estimation.

This study introduces a neural network approach to enhance the audio fidelity of poor-quality music, specifically targeting recordings with unwanted background noise and degraded high-frequency content. By utilizing a generator-discriminator framework, the proposed system is trained on a specialized dataset of recording pairs, each consisting of a low-quality track and its corresponding high-quality version, with the high-quality version serving as the target for restoration. Experimental evaluations indicate that the proposed model effectively restores spectral details and eliminates noise, resulting in a perceptually superior listening experience.

This paper introduces a technique for automatically generating realistic throwing animations by calculating how objects are thrown. While numerous physics-based animation systems exist, they often fail to account for the specific nuances of throwing actions. Drawing inspiration from human expertise, we developed a dataset of expert-throwing demonstrations using motion capture technology. Our analysis reveals that perceived realism in throwing depends on two key factors: the object's wobbling and the accuracy of the throw. We utilize this dataset to develop a novel, data-driven model for throwing that incorporates these realistic variations.

Syntax-Aware Attention (SAA) was introduced to flucency and fix semantic misalignment in neural machine translation (NMT) translation. This paper analyzes the impact of SAA on translation fluency and reorder errors. We find that SAA improves fluency by better preserving the original word order and mitigating semantic misalignment issues. Additionally, we observe a reduction in reorder errors, as SAA's attention mechanism aligns more closely with the source source structure, thereby enhancing the alignment of the generated translations. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating syntax-awareness into neural machine translation models for improved translation fluency and semantic alignment.

We have developed a new numerical code designed to calculate snow lines within protoplanetary discs. This tool is a valuable resource for planet formation simulations, as well as observational models aiming to interpret data from interferometers and ALMA. Our methodology employs a self-consistent approach to determine the snow line by simultaneously solving the disc's energy equation and the volatile species' temperature-dependent binding energy equation. We applied this method to study the snow lines of H2O, CO2, CO, and N2 across both classical Minimum Mass Solar Nebula (MMSN) disc models and the TW Hydrae disc. Our findings indicate that snow line positions are highly sensitive to variations in binding energy values; specifically, a factor of two variation in binding energy results in positional changes of up to a factor of three. Additionally, we examined the impact of accretion luminosity on these locations. Finally, we compared our results against previous studies and assessed their implications for interpreting observations of the accretion disc around TW Hydrae.

This paper introduces a new method for aligning statistical models with observed data through the use of divergence measures. By leveraging the flexibility of the generalized entropy framework, a new class of transformation-based divergence metrics is developed. These transformations are constructed by applying appropriate functions to the cumulative distribution functions of statistical distributions. These divergence metrics possess several desirable properties, such as satisfying the triangle inequality and allowing for adjustments of their parameters to theoretically match specific characteristics of empirical data distributions. In this study, the generalized transformation framework is applied to the Weibull distribution, yielding a subclass of transformation-based Weibull distributions. Estimation of the subclass parameters is conducted using maximum likelihood methods. Simulation experiments are performed to evaluate the performance of the new subclass and compare it against the standard Weibull distribution. Additionally, real-world data analysis is presented to demonstrate the practical application of the proposed subclass Weibull distribution.

We introduce a new approach to quantum state learning that relies on expressing observables as linear combinations of stabilizer measurements. By averaging the results of these measurements, we can calculate estimate values for expectations. This framework reduces the number of required distinct experiments to a polynomial rate relative to the number of qubits and a desired precision threshold. Furthermore, it offers a robust method for identifying symmetries within an unknown quantum state, thereby significantly lowering the complexity of preparing initial experimental setups. We also demonstrate the application of this framework to simulate Hamiltonians arising in quantum lattice gauge theories.

We refine asymptotic relationships for potentials with compact support in geometrical optics, and their application yields new estimates for compactly supported Fourier transforms at large scales. Additionally, these assumptions lead to improved bounds on the Agmon's and Littman's generalizations of the uncertainty principle.

We introduce a mutation method for one-class classification that targets outliers by transforming their labels into transmutations or mixtures. While transmutations assign a single class label to an outlier, a mixture transformation represents it as belonging to multiple classes simultaneously, which we achieve by setting the density values of several classes to a non-zero level for that class. We evaluate these approaches using the one-class classification variant of the Active Learning framework, demonstrating that our proposed methods are superior to baseline transmutation-only strategies on select datasets.

Sample-efficient methods are vital for accelerating the training of machine learning models, yet they often struggle with multi-task linear regression because tasks sharing similar data can interfere with one another, hindering convergence. Although recent research has addressed this issue, it remains unclear how to achieve sample efficiency without making restrictive assumptions about task relationships. This work introduces a novel algorithm that is both sample-efficient and capable of handling arbitrary configurations of shared parameters. The algorithm leverages a new loss function that incorporates a carefully selected convex combination of tasks to guide optimization. Crucially, this approach does not require prior knowledge of the loss function's parameters, as they are automatically determined by a simple iterative process. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the proposed method converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$, where $t$ represents time, using only a minimal number of samples. Empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets confirm that the method outperforms existing approaches in terms of sample efficiency.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across numerous natural language tasks, yet their deployment is frequently hindered by high computational costs. This study evaluates two quantization strategies—Knowledge Distillation (KD) and post-training quantization (PTQ)—across 149 languages to assess their efficacy in zero-shot settings. Our findings indicate that while KD generally outperforms PTQ for high-resource languages, both methods exhibit comparable performance on low-resource and undocuted languages. Furthermore, we observe a correlation between source language families and model effectiveness in multilingual scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach incorporating a universal language identifier within the KD framework, which yields significant gains for PTQ across various low-resource settings.

In this study, we address a query posed by Balogh, Bar\^n, and Schacht regarding the Tur\`an density of $k$-path-free graphs within $r$-uniform structures. Building upon the work of Baber and Talbot, who identified the $k=3$ case for $r=4$ by analyzing a specific extremal construction, we introduce a novel approach to determine the Tur\`an density for $k=5$ across all even values of $r$. Our methodology involves a two-tiered framework: first, we employ a density iteration technique to construct a specific $T_r(k)$-free graph model, and second, we utilize a flag algebra to demonstrate that the edge density of any large, uniformly pseudorandom $T_r(k)$-free graph remains bounded by the density of our constructed model.

Detecting pneumonia in chest X-ray (CxR) radiographs is a critical yet difficult task that relies heavily on expert knowledge, resulting in substantial costs for data annotation. This study introduces a method to mitigate these expenses by employing image transformations to generate diverse views of limited radiographs, thereby reducing the demand for manually labeled data. Our approach utilizes a pre-trained model trained on the CheXpert dataset to predict the likelihood of a new image being human-labeled; it then selects specific images for expert verification based on this prediction. Consequently, radiographs with high uncertainty receive expert validation, whereas those with low uncertainty are automatically classified as negative for pneumonia. We evaluate this strategy using a ResNet-50 model on the INATLTX dataset, demonstrating that our proposed method can decrease labeling requirements by up to 90% while maintaining performance levels comparable to models trained on the entire dataset.

Although image captioning has advanced significantly, it still suffers from the need for extensive pre-trained models and a reliance on manually crafted prompts. This work introduces a novel approach integrating prompt learning directly into the captioning framework. By embedding visual features into prompt sequences, we generate an intermediate feature representation that serves as the foundation for the final caption generation. This method eliminates the necessity for external pre-trained models and automatically derives prompts from the input data. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed technique surpasses current state-of-the-art models on the MS COCO benchmark, achieving an improvement of 0.7 BLEU-4 score. Furthermore, we observe notable performance gains on the Flickr30k and Flickr8k datasets.

Contrastive forms of causation are essential for evaluating harm and benefit based on both utility and actual outcomes. This paper examines the link between contrastive causation and these three elements—utility, outcomes, and their interaction—while also exploring the relationship between contrastive and non-contrastive statements regarding causation. We propose a formal framework for analyzing this model and demonstrate its application through several illustrative cases.

Wildlife monitoring is a cornerstone of wildlife conservation, yet it faces significant hurdles due to the high costs and labor required for field data collection. This study examines how deep learning can enhance monitoring efficiency by analyzing camera trap imagery to detect and classify wildlife. We introduce a novel approach that leverages the spatial context of the camera trap setup to boost detection accuracy. Our method employs a specialized deep learning model to identify animals and assess their bounding boxes within the frame. By incorporating the known location of each camera trap as an auxiliary input, the model filters out irrelevant areas of the image, thereby improving prediction performance. We evaluated our approach using the WildCATs dataset, achieving a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.755. These findings indicate that integrating spatial context yields superior results compared to baseline models, demonstrating the viability of this strategy for real-world wildlife monitoring applications.

Although most current zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) translation methods rely on few-shot learning, we introduce two new approaches for few-shot TTS translation that function effectively even without using support shots. Our first method employs a generative adversarial framework where a TTS model is trained via Generative Adversarial Distillation (GAD) using a high-quality reference model, which is pre-trained on extensive multilingual datasets. Our second method utilizes an embedding-based approach that projects query embeddings from an in-domain large language model to a universal speech embedding space, which is subsequently decoded by a TTS model. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that both approaches significantly boost performance in few-shot TTS translation scenarios and also yield notable improvements over existing zero-shot methods.

This study examines the impact of fading memory on the formulation of a novel class of heat conduction equations. By employing the fractional derivative operator, which characterizes the system's memory, we establish the fractional heat conduction equation. This development relies on the identification of a suitable constitutive relation involving a fractional integral operator. Consequently, the resulting model yields the dual-phase-lag (DPL) equation featuring fractional derivatives. Furthermore, the model is validated by demonstrating that it reduces to established fractional and classical heat conduction theories under specific limiting conditions. Finally, the physical implications of the DPL equation with fractional derivatives are analyzed.

Accurately projecting peak energy loads is vital for grid stability and security, yet current forecasting methods often produce significant errors during these critical periods. This study introduces a novel approach that integrates conventional energy forecasts with dedicated peak forecasts to enhance load prediction precision. By utilizing a fusion formula, the proposed model merges the smoothed output of standard forecasting techniques with the refined results of specialized peak forecasting. Experimental evaluations using the Wavelet-LSTM framework on real-world energy datasets demonstrate that this hybrid strategy substantially surpasss existing single-method approaches in accuracy during peak hours.

Recent advancements in machine learning have yielded remarkable achievements, yet these results often demand extensive computational resources and large-scale datasets. To address this limitation, this study examines the potential performance gains achievable by integrating knowledge into machine learning algorithms. Specifically, we investigate the application of the Fourier Transform—a well-established signal processing tool—to a convolutional neural network (CNN) for image classification tasks. By embedding the Fourier Transform within the CNN architecture, we create a hybrid model that leverages domain expertise alongside data-driven learning. Our experiments, conducted on the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets, demonstrate that this hybrid approach surpasses the accuracy of standard convolutional neural networks while utilizing fewer training samples. These findings underscore the efficacy of the proposed method and highlight the broader promise of incorporating external knowledge to enhance machine learning efficiency and effectiveness.

Although deep learning has significantly advanced the field of automatic lesion localization, it still relies on expensive pixel-level annotations. This paper introduces a data-driven approach that relies solely on image-level labels to estimate lesion probability, utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) to convert this data into pseudo segmentation maps. Furthermore, a specialized loss function is designed to enhance the discriminator's ability to identify discrepancies between these reconstructed maps and ground truth. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate that the generated pseudo-segmentations achieve an average Dice similarity coefficient of 0.812, indicating that the proposed method can effectively localize lesions without the need for pixel-level labels.

This study introduces a proposed approach for identifying vertebrae in CT scans, which addresses the limitations of existing techniques that often yield inaccurate results due to label scarcity and misalignments. The approach employs a two-stage framework: first, a two-dimensional convolutional neural network screens for vertebrae and determines their orientation, while subsequently, a graph-based model refines the bounding boxes by leveraging mutual supervision from the initial identification and alignment tasks. Experimental evaluations on a new spine dataset demonstrate that the method achieves an identification accuracy of 98.1% and a 45.4% relative improvement in mean absolute error for localization compared to the best competing approaches.

By integrating a quantum dot with an optical cavity, researchers can observe the complex interplay between light and matter. The proposed method utilizes a second probe cavity to monitor changes in the reflected light, which is sensitive to the polariton formation. This technique helps in understanding how vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field affect the polariton stability. Spring-based actuators offer a highly efficient method for legged locomotion by storing and releasing elastic potential energy through controlled deformation. However, these systems are difficult to model accurately and can exhibit unpredictable, nonlinear behaviors that complicate control. This study introduces a data-driven approach to control such systems by integrating them into a framework known as the Data-Driven Legged Locomotion (D3LO). In this approach, a legged robot equipped with spring-based limbs is modeled using a linear state-space system, with parameters identified through least-squares optimization from recorded state trajectories. The resulting controller, designed via a Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) structure, is synthesized using a learned disturbance model and a learned cost function. Experimental results from D3LO running on a two-legged robot prototype demonstrate the approach's efficacy, achieving an average of 1.62 meters per stride and completing 100 consecutive strides at a speed of 0.5 meters per second.

Although current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors are not yet capable of executing full eigenstate analysis of arbitrary multi-qubit systems, they can effectively address specific facets of the separability problem for certain quantum states. We demonstrate that a restricted set of eigenvalues can be computed on these devices to evaluate a specific entanglement witness tailored for detecting a particular state's separability. Furthermore, we outline strategies to mitigate measurement inaccuracies arising from device noise.

The effects of electron finite Larmor radius (FLR) effects on tearing mode parity in the context of the magnetic reconnection instability within a collisionless plasma have been examined. The analysis focuses on a two-dimensional, electrostatic tearing problem in the collisionless regime, utilizing the Harris current sheet as a model. The findings indicate that the inclusion of electron FLR effects shifts the fine-scale tearing parity from odd to even. This shift arises from the emergence of a new solution to the two-dimensional Poisson equation in the even parity configuration, which remains independent of collisionality. The presence of this even parity solution allows for electrostatic potential structures consistent with the finite electron gyroradius scale. The study further explores the implications of this parity change on the characteristics of the fine-scale tearing mode in collisionless plasmas. The findings suggest that the even parity tearing mode may be more prevalent in certain plasma conditions, which could have significant implications for understanding magnetic reconnection processes in astrophysical and laboratory plasmas. Fashion Instance-level Image Retrieval (FIR) aims to locate images of identical fashion items from extensive repositories, a capability that is highly valuable for practical applications like virtual dressing rooms and online shopping. However, existing methods often fail to achieve satisfactory performance due to two main challenges: first, they rely on pre-trained models that are ill-suited for FIR, leading to a lack of specific visual features; second, they suffer from severe negative sample interference, as most existing approaches retrieve irrelevant items that degrade retrieval accuracy. To address these issues, we introduce ViFIR, a novel method that combines a specific architecture with an effective retrieval strategy. Specifically, we employ a lightweight, trainable model, Lightweight Feature Extractor (LFE), to generate robust representations. Furthermore, we propose a new framework, Negative Relevance Feedback (NRF), designed to mitigate the impact of negative samples. Experimental results on public FIR benchmarks confirm that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the convergence behavior of truncated gradient flow methods applied to infinite-dimensional ill-posed problems. By analyzing a specific class of non-linear evolution equations regularized through time truncation, we demonstrate that the approximation error of these regularized solutions can be minimized by selecting an optimal stopping time. This finding is supported by numerical experiments that validate the theoretical results. Furthermore, we show that this optimal stopping rule can be computed efficiently using a coupled adjoint state system.

We introduce a new cost constructor tailored for depth estimation from multiple views, specifically addressing the challenge of handling occlusions. By utilizing a proposed deep network, our method effectively aggregates features across diverse spatial and semantic dimensions to enhance cost map quality. To resolve occlusions, we implement a back-propagation strategy that dynamically adjusts contributions based on pixel reliability, ensuring that information from occluded areas has minimal influence on the final output. Experiments conducted on the CUBES and SceneNet RF benchmarks demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance compared to existing methods. We present DDF-based Fock-space representations for the S-matrix in bosonic string theory, applicable to systems interacting with massless fields under arbitrary backgrounds. These representations are explicitly constructed for the gauged little group corresponding to specific asymptotic symmetries within the bulk framework, encompassing standard gravity as well as the recently theorized ghostly gravities. By utilizing the recently derived soft graviton theorem in the bulk, we establish soft asymptotic symmetries for these bulk theories, demonstrating that the corresponding charges also admit soft representations.

This study introduces a channel load-aware selection mechanism for mobile home WiFi networks, which enhances throughput and reduces delay by accounting for channel load during network association. Unlike traditional methods that rely solely on Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI), our approach dynamically assesses channel load to facilitate seamless transitions between channels. We validate the efficacy of our channel load-aware selection framework through extensive simulations, which demonstrate that our protocol outperforms conventional selection techniques.
